requirements.text: The Bash guard refuses, on a build or fix lease, an inline interpreter program (python, node, perl, ruby and the other interpreters it reads, from a heredoc or a -c/-e argument) whose file-writing call names its target through a variable, an expression or another call rather than a literal path, saying the guard cannot read where the program writes and naming the fix (a literal path, or the Edit tool); a literal path is judged as today, and a program that writes nothing passes (F323: on 2026-10-27 two Devs' python heredocs wrote protected check files through a variable, unseen by the guard)

rules.text: in every program text the guard reads (the -c/-e code arguments of an interpreter command and the body of a heredoc fed to one), a call head program_writes reads as a write whose target argument is not a string literal (it starts with a name, a $, a parenthesis, an f-string prefix, a backtick template holding ${, a dot or any token other than a plain quote) is refused under a run lease; for open, a non-literal mode argument is refused the same way

the reason's first line is the call as written in the program (from its head through the closing parenthesis of its arguments) followed by ' writes a file the guard cannot name: the program gives its target through a variable, an expression or another call, so the guard cannot read where it writes', and its last line is 'Next: name the file as a literal path in the program, or write it with the Edit tool (Write for a new file)'; the systemMessage shows the user the first line

the rule holds for an agent of the owning session on both inline forms of every interpreter the guard reads (python3 -c, python -c, node -e, perl -e, ruby -e, php -r, lua -e, deno eval, bun -e; python3 - <<EOF and node <<EOF heredocs), under build, fix, qa, map and plan leases; outside a run programs are not judged

the R76 order is kept: a literal path outside the plan gets the R76 refusal naming the path, judged before any unreadable target of the same program; a literal path inside the plan passes; an unreadable target is refused even when lease.files is null (any project file allowed)

a program that writes nothing (print, json.load(open(p)), open(p), open(p, 'r'), open(p, 'rb'), fs.readFileSync(p), Path(p).read_text()), a heredoc with the same text fed to cat or tee, a script file run by name and a string method on a bare variable receiver (s.replace, s.rename) pass

the Bash guard's block of a program writing a file it cannot name ends with its next step, as a line of the 'every block of the file guard and the Bash guard ends with its next step' case of tests/refusal-next-step.bats

the guard-bash.jq header states the rule beside the heredoc-as-data rule (D281), and tools/bench-hooks.sh's interp.json program writes a literal path and a path held in a variable, so the measured 'guard (interp)' cases hold both shapes

docs/guards.md's 'Programs that write files' paragraph states the rule in place of the guard-rail sentence (a write whose target the guard cannot read is refused with the fix named; a program that writes nothing passes; a script file run by name is not read); docs/workflows.md's refusal table has a Guards row for it whose Next cell is the guard's words; plugin/agents/dev.md's 'Write only inside the project' line says files are written with the Edit and Write tools and a program that writes names its file as a literal path, because the guard cannot read another target

requirements.text: vbw apply refuses, naming the check and the file, a check whose command filters a test file by case name (bats --filter PATTERN) when the pattern matches no case name in the file as committed: the Lead writes the failing cases at planning, so a new check is red because its cases fail, never because none exist (M45, 2026-10-27: four of nine new checks were red on an empty match and the Devs had to write the cases during the build, into protected files)

rules.text: in every mode (full apply, --add, --patch), judged on the document's checks after the merge and after the two-owner and mixed-owner judgments, a check whose argv command (env and timeout wrappers skipped) is bats with a case filter (--filter PATTERN, --filter=PATTERN or -f PATTERN) whose pattern, an unanchored extended regular expression (grep -E -e), matches no @test name of the .bats files the argv names, as they stand in the project folder at apply time, is refused before anything changes, with the mode's name; the record is byte-identical and the runner never runs

the words are 'C9 runs tests/x.bats with a case filter (--filter 'R220') that matches no case name in the file: the Lead writes the failing cases at planning, so a new check is red because its cases fail, never because none exist', and the refusal ends 'Next: write the cases the filter names into tests/x.bats (each @test name matching the pattern), see them fail with the runner, then send the document again; or correct the pattern'

a test file missing from the project folder counts as one with no case names and is named 'FILE (missing)'; a pattern grep -E cannot parse matches nothing and is named; several files, or the .bats files directly under a directory word, are named comma-separated and a match in any one passes; a pattern matching at least one case passes

a check without a filter, a runner that is not bats (pytest -k, go test -run), --filter-tags and --filter-status are not judged; -f and --filter= are judged like --filter, behind env and timeout wrappers too; a check the document resends unchanged is judged on the file as it stands; the two-owner and mixed-owner refusals keep their precedence
every mode's refusal of an empty filter ends with a Next line of its own, never the fallback arm's, and apply_next fed the message directly answers with the empty-filter arm naming the file

the Lead's brief rule 6 Lean checks line says the filter names cases the file already holds, written at planning before vbw apply, because vbw apply refuses a bats case filter that matches no case name and a Dev cannot add them later (check files are protected during the build)

docs/workflows.md's list of what vbw apply refuses names the empty-filter refusal (the check, the file, the reason: red because its cases fail, never because none exist) and its 'Every refusal and its next step' table has a row whose Next cell is the kernel's words; docs/proof.md's Checks section says a case filter must match a case in the file at apply time

requirements.text: The proof's scope check chooses the record version a commit is judged against by git ancestry (the last record commit that is an ancestor of the judged commit), never by commit time, so a record commit that shares a second with a plan commit cannot make the later version the base and report a false violation; a regression test pins two commits in the same second with GIT_COMMITTER_DATE (#715, halindrome, 2026-10-29; seen as the flaky scope-of-its-time case in CI)

rules.text: the record version a flagged commit is judged against is the last commit of .vbw/record.json that is an ancestor of it in git history, never the one nearest in clock time
the versions 'since' are that base and the versions after it in the record's own history
a record commit in the same second as the plan commit, whose version no longer allows the plan's file, is not the base: no violation is reported
a record commit made after the plan commit but stamped earlier (a clock set back) is still after it: no violation is reported
a file no version since the base allows stays a violation, and a decision naming the commit and the file accepts it and no other: the four earlier cases pass unchanged
finding the base costs at most one git process per distinct flagged commit, never a walk of the whole history per candidate
docs/proof.md's Scope step says the base is the last record commit the judged commit descends from and no longer describes picking it by time

requirements.text: The hook and status line benchmarks judge each case against a reference measured on the same runner in the same run (the absolute budgets, 20 ms and 60 ms, stay the documented meaning on a nominal runner), so a uniformly slow runner, where shell and jq startup stay under the busy threshold yet every case runs at half speed, reports slow, not failed, and a real regression of one case still fails; the bench output names the reference and the ratio (#716, halindrome; F327: the 2.1.18 and 2.1.19 CI runs failed Linux shards on runner speed with the guard unchanged)

rules.text: the bench measures one fixed reference workload (a jq program of fixed size over fixed input, run as the hooks are) on the same machine in the same run, before any case is judged

it prints once the line `reference: <X> ms CPU per call; nominal <N> ms (an M1 Max Mac and GitHub's macOS runner, ...); ratio <R>`, naming the measured cost, the nominal cost pinned in the script and the ratio to two decimals

at a ratio of 1 or less every case is judged against its absolute budget (20 ms per guard call, 60 ms status line, 10 ms hand-back) with today's lines: a fast machine gets no looser and no tighter budget

at a ratio above 1 a case above its absolute budget but at or under budget times ratio prints its line on stdout marked slow, naming the cost, the absolute budget, the ratio and the scaled budget, and the bench exits 0
at a ratio above 1 a case above budget times ratio prints ': OVER' on stderr and the bench exits 1: a real regression still fails on a slow machine
the measure-again rule (D517) judges the second measure against the scaled budget and its line names that budget
VBW_BENCH_REFERENCE_MS stands in for the measured reference, as VBW_HOOK_BUDGET_MS stands in for a limit
the busy rule is unchanged: sh and jq startup alone above the hook limit reports busy, judges nothing and exits 0
CI sets no stand-in reference and no CI-only limit, so the release run's benchmark shard shows the reference line and a slow runner is never a failed shard
docs/guards.md's Budget bullet, docs/statusline.md and CLAUDE.md's hot-path rule state the reference, the ratio and the slow report, with the absolute budgets as the meaning on a nominal machine

requirements.text: jq 1.7 is the floor: vbw doctor refuses jq below 1.7 naming the installed version and how to get a current jq (the jq releases page; on Debian 12 the bookworm-backports package), README.md and docs state the floor, and no kernel jq relies on behaviour that differs between 1.7 and 1.8 (#709, halindrome: jq 1.6's contains("\u0000") is true for every string, so the record's argv rule rejected every check, and an if without else did not compile; support of 1.6 declined 2026-10-29)

rules.text: vbw doctor with a jq below 1.7 prints a fail line naming the installed version and 1.7 as the floor
its fix line names the jq releases page (github.com/jqlang/jq/releases) and, for Debian 12, `apt install -t bookworm-backports jq`
jq 1.7.0, 1.7.1 and 1.8.x each pass doctor as `jq <version>`
a missing jq keeps the `jq is missing` line: doctor does not die on it
every vbw command but doctor refuses a jq below 1.7 before doing anything: doctor's one-line message with its fix on stderr, exit non-zero, nothing written (vbw init creates no .vbw folder)
the check is one jq --version per kernel command, after the libraries load and before the dispatch; vbw doctor itself still runs its fuller report
the hooks and the status line gain no version check: none of them asks jq its version

the plugin passes the scan (plugin/lib/failing-tests.jq defines its own trim)

requirements.text: The router chooses the spec's `## Commands` from the map's Tests section: a command the map ran and dated is preferred; a whole suite the map marked "Not run" is never put in `## Commands` silently, the router runs it once (its own step, before planning) or proposes it to the user marked unverified; a suite that fails today, as the map or that run shows, is named to the user before planning with the narrower command as the recommendation; `plugin/skills/vibe/SKILL.md` and `plugin/skills/map/SKILL.md` say so and tests pin the wording (#733, halindrome, 2026-10-30: two Angular suites the map had not run went into the contract and one was red)

rules.text: the mapping workflow's merge prompt tells the Lead to mark every test or lint command in the Tests section `ran as of <short commit>, <date>: <what happened, how long it took>` when a scout ran it, or `Not run` when none did
the map skill says what the two marks mean, that the router chooses ## Commands from them, and still never writes .vbw/map.md itself
the spec step chooses ## Commands from the map's Tests section and prefers a command the map ran and dated; sub-project, interpreter and recommend stay

a whole suite marked Not run is never written into ## Commands silently: before planning, one AskUserQuestion per such suite names it as unverified with the expected time (or that it is unknown) and offers run it now (Recommended), leave it out and use only the verified commands, add it unverified; under hands-off the router takes run it now and says so

run it now is its own step before any planning run: the suite runs once (a long one in the background, its whole result read), the user hears green or red with the failing tests' names, and the dated outcome is recorded with vbw decide (Commands: <command> ran <date> at <short commit>: green|red (<n> failing)), never by editing .vbw/map.md

a suite that fails today, by the map's dated result or the run just made, is named before planning with the narrower command (one-test-file form or the sub-project's green command) recommended; it enters ## Commands only on the user's choice, the router then says the first proof will be red, and the chosen lines are written under ## Commands followed by vbw spec sync

tools/l3-suite.sh has the mapnotrun scenario in ALL and its header: two suites, one the map ran green and one the map did not run and which is red today; it passes when ## Commands holds only the green (or narrower) command and a dated decision names the red suite, judged in .vbw/spec.md, the record and the transcripts' tool calls

requirements.text: Suggestions (`vbw:suggest`) are offered right after triage adds requirements to the active milestone, before the first planning run, so a yes costs nothing; and a suggestion at plan approval that would add a requirement states what a yes costs (a new planning run, with the kernel's estimate from `vbw next`) and offers "add to this milestone (replan)" or "add to the backlog" (`vbw todo add`), the backlog as the recommendation; the suggest, triage and vibe skills say so and tests pin the wording (#734, halindrome: 26 of 52 planning minutes were replans after approval-time yeses)

rules.text: vbw next --json at the approve step carries detail.replan: the sentence for a planning run of the open requirements plus one, built as step.say is for a plan step, reading 'Planning the work: about N min, until around HH:MM' with history
with fewer than 3 planning steps in the history detail.replan reads 'Planning the work: no end time yet (VBW has timed fewer than 3 steps like this here)'
detail.replan exists at no step but approve: the plan and build steps carry no such field
the triage skill's now outcome follows vbw:suggest once after the ideas are added, before the first planning run; a now idea during a run waits for the run to end
the suggest skill names its three moments (spec proposal, right after triage adds requirements, plan approval) in its description and under When, and still never offers mid-run or mid-build

at plan approval a suggestion that would add a requirement states the cost of a yes from detail.replan (a new planning run) and offers add to the backlog (Recommended, vbw todo add --sort next --size <small|medium|large>), add to this milestone (replan) or no; a choice or constraint (vbw decide) costs no replan; at spec proposal and after triage the answers stay Yes/No because a yes costs nothing there

the router offers suggestions at the spec step, at the approve step (passing detail.replan to vbw:suggest as the cost of a yes) and after triage adds work, and nowhere else (build, fix, qa, prove, run)
the docs for the suggest and triage skills say the three moments and the priced yes with the backlog recommended

requirements.text: `vbw mutate PLAN --run` refuses, with a Next line naming the running one, to start while another `--run` of the same plan is still running, through a per-plan marker in `.vbw/runtime` that a dead process does not hold, so two runs of one plan never make their own copies and compete for slots; the Dev's instructions say how to wait for a long run (start it in the background and read its result) (#738, halindrome: a run past Claude Code's 600 s limit was followed by a second run of the same plan)

rules.text: vbw mutate PLAN --run takes the per-plan marker .vbw/runtime/mutate-queue/PLAN/run.pid holding its own pid before it reads any queue entry, and removes it when the run ends, on success, on a survivor and on a refusal

a second --run while the marker's pid is alive exits non-zero before reading, copying or deleting any queue entry and before recording anything, with a line beginning vbw: that names the running one (its pid and the command) and a Next: line telling the Dev to wait for it to finish and never start a second run
a marker whose pid is dead, empty or not a number does not block: the next run takes it over, holds its own pid while the breaks run and leaves no marker after
two --run of the same plan never both make copies: while the first holds its slot the second is refused, exactly one set of proof copies exists, and each queue entry is recorded once
the marker lives only under .vbw/runtime and mutate-queue.sh's header comment names run.pid

the Dev agent's instructions say to start a long --run in the background on purpose (the 10-minute one-command limit), wait for it and read its whole result, never start a second --run of the same plan, and that a refusal naming a running one means wait
docs/workflows.md documents the refusal with its Next: wait for it to finish wording, the run.pid marker, the dead-marker takeover and the background advice

requirements.text: The bench's reference workload has the guard's shape, one jq call that reads a JSON document of fixed size with a program of fixed size, so its ratio tracks the hooks' startup-and-parse-bound cost on every runner; the nominal figure is remeasured for the new shape on the Mac, GitHub's macOS figure read from the pull request's shard-1 log before merge and the larger pinned, and the reference line keeps its form (T201: on PR #739 the Ubuntu 26.04 runner measured ratio 0.90 while every guard case read 21 ms against 20)

rules.text: the bench's reference workload is one jq call of the guard's shape (--rawfile glance, --arg root, --arg dir, --arg open, -f PROGRAM - DOCUMENT END) over the bench's own program and document, never the shipped guard, a project file or the old counting program

the reference program and document are deterministic and of the sizes the provenance states (their proportion to the shipped guard is R233's rule): the document a JSON object of at least 50 KB, the guard-shaped call runs on them, and VBW_BENCH_REFERENCE_FILES=DIR writes them for inspection

the provenance comment names the shape and the two sizes in bytes, the M1 Max figures from five runs dated on or after 2026-10-31 and GitHub's figure from the shard-1 log; NOMINAL_MS is a number and NOMINAL_WHEN names a month
docs/guards.md describes the reference workload as a guard-shaped jq call over a fixed document and program

requirements.text: The R207 case 'the figures are measured' in tests/mutate-time.bats holds without a real elapsed second: the clock mutate's timer reads is injected in the test (a clock file or variable prooftime reads when set, as a test may set the proof's), and the case asserts the figures from injected readings; no test file outside tests/timed-*.bats asserts elapsed time (T195: the case failed on Linux runners in the 2.1.19, 2.1.20 and #736 CI runs with unbroken and break both at 1.1 s)

with VBW_PROOFTIME_CLOCK unset or naming an unreadable file, the machine clock is read as before (nanos, perl or whole seconds)

the figures-are-measured case runs vbw with the injected clock, a check on broken code moving it by 1.000 s, and asserts break R1.1 = 1.0, unbroken = 0.0, the total 1.0 and the sum, without a real second
tests/mutate-time.bats pauses the shell nowhere (no sleep) and reads no clock, so the default run measures no duration
docs/proof.md names VBW_PROOFTIME_CLOCK as a test hook

phases.title: The start-of-project interview, asked once
phases.goal: At the start of a project (after mapping for existing code) VBW asks the three fixed questions, what is being built and for whom, up to three written follow-ups, and then where to keep the personal answers, and never asks again.
criteria: For a new project the router, before spec work, asks the three fixed questions in order with exactly the listed options; for an existing codebase the interview comes after mapping.
After the three, VBW asks briefly what the user is building and for whom; the answer is written into the spec Goals.
VBW then asks at most three follow-up questions it writes for that user's level and this project; zero follow-ups is allowed, four never.
The last question asks where to keep the personal answers (private on this machine, or saved in the project for everyone); VBW applies the choice via P30's command.
Once answers exist, the interview is never asked again in that project, including after a new session or a new milestone.
A project started before this version (milestones present, no answers) is asked once, at its next milestone start, not in the middle of a run or phase.
If the user declines or gives an unrecognised answer to a fixed question, VBW re-asks that question or records a stated default; it never records an invalid value.

An alone check waits for running non-alone checks to finish, and non-alone checks wait while an alone check runs; non-alone checks still run in parallel with each other
The same holds across vbw check, vbw prove and the checks run by vbw fix done and vbw commit, since all go through the one check runner
A check killed or timed out while holding the exclusion releases it; a crashed vbw process leaves no stale lock that blocks later checks (a lock owned by a dead process is taken over)
A wait that exceeds a bounded limit fails with a message naming the check being waited on, not a hang
Checks of two different projects (or worktrees with separate .vbw) do not block each other

Without an alone marker on any check, behaviour and timing are unchanged and all existing tests pass
The docs (docs/proof.md or the contract docs) describe the alone marker; kernel stays under the 3,300 line budget

vbw fix done on a fix whose served checks all have a recorded pass with the same file fingerprint and the same contract hash does not execute them, and prints for each that the check is unchanged since its pass and when that pass was

A check whose last result was fail or timeout, or that never ran, is rerun, never skipped
A check with no declared files or whose served files cannot be fingerprinted is always rerun
Uncommitted changes in the fix's files still block closing as before (dirty-file refusal unchanged); the skip applies only to the check rerun
vbw prove runs every check regardless of recorded passes, and a failing check still fails the proof

Records written by earlier versions without a recorded pass read fine and simply rerun checks (R33 compatibility, schema version handling checked); the new fields are validated by the single record writer
Fix closing outcomes (fixed or closed for [human]) are identical to before when checks are skipped

phases.goal: After a round of fixes, QA checks again only the phases that did not pass, the phases whose own inputs changed since they passed, and the phases that build on a re-checked phase; every other phase keeps its pass.
criteria: Each QA pass stores one digest of the phase's own inputs (its files and tests as committed, its goal and plan, and the digests of the phases it builds on) in the existing qa.tree field; no new record field, the record schema is unchanged (D91); the per-input digests that name a reason are this clone's cache in $(git common dir)/vbw/qa.json

A change to a file that belongs to no phase re-checks no phase.

Dependency rule: a phase that builds on a phase that is re-checked because its inputs changed is also re-checked, even when its own inputs are unchanged; it is transitive (A, then B on A, then C on B all re-check).

phases.title: Proof re-runs only the checks whose files changed
phases.goal: vbw prove runs again only the checks whose files, or whose approved definition, changed since they last passed, reuses every other passing result, and tells the user which results it reused.
criteria: A check counts as unchanged only when both of these match its last passing result: its approved definition (the check's run command, expected exit, expected output, timeout, alone flag and file list) and the committed content of its served files. Served files are the check's own files plus the files of every plan that serves its requirement. This is the existing check fingerprint (D181); no new ledger or state file is added.
After a proof in which every check passed, a commit that changes only a file served by check A makes the next vbw prove run A again and reuse the result of every check that does not serve that file.
A check whose last result was fail, timeout or lost runs again, even when none of its files changed.

After a proof in which one check failed and the others passed, the next vbw prove runs the failed check plus any check whose served files changed, and reuses the other passes, even though that earlier proof as a whole did not pass.
A check that declares no files runs on every vbw prove and is never reused.
A check with a served path that is not in the committed code (HEAD) runs on every vbw prove and is never reused.

When one check's approved definition changes and the contract is approved again, that check runs again. A check whose definition and served files are unchanged is reused, even though the contract as a whole changed.
A file changed in the working folder but not committed does not make a check run again (the proof runs on a clean copy of the committed code, R32), and it is never counted as proven.
An interrupted proof (the unfinished marker is left behind) means the next vbw prove reuses nothing and runs every check.
A second vbw prove with no commit since the passing-proof commit still runs everything fresh (D173).

A reused result keeps the time it really ran. vbw prove prints it as reused, with that time, on the check's own line, and also prints one line saying how many checks ran and how many were reused. vbw show evidence marks it reused as well.
Project commands keep the existing reuse rule (R103): a command's result is reused only when the committed code is the same as at the proof that passed it, and its approved argv is unchanged.
docs/proof.md explains, in plain words, which checks run again, which are reused, and why a check with no declared files always runs.
Tests cover each case above, and the existing proof-reuse and fix-close tests still pass.

phases.title: A quick test command for build rounds, a full proof for QA and shipping
phases.goal: Build and fix rounds can use a project's faster test command. QA verdicts and shipping are accepted only after a full proof (vbw prove --full) that ran every check and every full project command.
criteria: A project names its quick test command as a Commands entry called `quick` in .vbw/spec.md, for example `- quick: bash tools/test.sh --quick`. It needs approval like any other command. VBW never detects or suggests one (D180), and a project without one behaves as it does today.
When a quick command is named and approved, a plain vbw prove runs it in place of the test command and runs every other project command as before. The test command does not run.
When a quick command is named but not approved, a plain vbw prove runs the full test command instead, so a build round never goes untested. The summary says the quick command was not approved.

vbw prove --full reuses nothing. It runs every approved check, the test command and every other project command, but not the quick command, so nothing runs twice. vbw prove with any other argument is refused with the usage line.

The evidence records whether the proof was full. It is full only when every check and every full project command ran in that proof: none reused, and the quick command not used in place of the test command. A plain vbw prove that happened to run all of them counts as full.
vbw qa record refuses a proof that is not full, without changing the record, and its message says to run vbw prove --full. The existing refusal when the code changed since the proof still applies.
vbw ship refuses a proof that is not full, without changing the record, and its message says to run vbw prove --full.

When the next step would be QA or shipping and the latest proof is not full, vbw next asks for a proof and says to run vbw prove --full (the --json detail marks it as full). The /vbw:vibe router then runs vbw prove --full, so a normal run never reaches a refusal.

The QA agent's and the verifying workflow's instruction for a refused verdict says to run vbw prove --full, then try the record once more. The test-command result given to QA agents comes from the full proof's test command, never from the quick command.
The vbw prove summary says whether the proof was full or partial.

VBW's own project follows D179: tools/test.sh has a quick mode that runs shellcheck, the engineering rules and the core test files, but not the files approved checks already run and not the timing benchmarks. VBW's spec names that mode as its `quick` command.
docs/proof.md and the user docs explain the quick command, when a full proof is needed, and the two refusal messages.
Tests cover each case above, including a project without a quick command, an unapproved quick command, and a refusal followed by a successful vbw prove --full and record.

phases.title: Triage of every new request
phases.goal: Each new idea brought to /vbw:vibe is sorted on one line as now, next or later, with a reason and a size, before any planning; the user confirms or overrules it in the same menu, an overrule gets one plain warning and a recorded reason, and the outcome is in the record.

When /vbw:vibe receives a new request, before any requirement is added, any planning starts or any file changes, the user sees one line per idea: the sort (now: it joins the active milestone; next or later: it goes into the backlog), the reason in one sentence, and the size (small, medium or large).
That line is inside one AskUserQuestion menu whose first option is VBW's sort marked (Recommended) and whose other options are the two other sorts; no typed command is asked of the user.

A message that is not a new idea gets no triage: an answer to a question VBW asked, 'continue' or 'go on', an approval, or a request that already matches an existing requirement or open backlog item (that one is named instead, and VBW offers to move a backlog item to now).

Confirmed or chosen 'next' or 'later': the idea is added with vbw todo, and vbw todo list shows its sort and size; next items are listed before later items; backlog items added before this change still list, without a sort or size, and nothing about them changes.
The triage does not interrupt a running build or check: a request that arrives during a run is sorted, and a 'now' idea waits for the run to end before planning picks it up.
Triage happens at every autonomy setting (guided, balanced, hands-off), because the user has just typed the request and is present.

When the user picks a sort other than VBW's, VBW asks exactly one follow-up question (decision D207) that says plainly what the choice displaces and its risk (for example: 'now' grows the milestone, sends the plan back for planning and a new approval, and delays the work already planned; 'later' instead of 'now' leaves a problem VBW judged urgent unfixed), with options: one or two ready reasons, the user's own words, or keep VBW's sorting.

phases.title: Arm the loop: start, stop, status, and approval by delegation
phases.goal: The user hands named backlog items to the loop with a spending limit, and from then on the kernel approves a contract made of exactly those items on the user's behalf, records that it did, and still makes every other contract wait for the user.
criteria: vbw loop start ITEM... with a ceiling choice records the loop in the project (the kernel is the only writer, so the loop lives in .vbw/record.json and is committed): the items in the order given, each item's text as the backlog records it at that moment (a snapshot, so a later edit of the backlog changes nothing), the ceiling and its mode, the session that started it, the start time, and the cost figures of every known session at that moment as the loop's baseline (its starting point for spend). vbw loop status prints all of it from any session of the project.

The ceiling is the user's choice at start (D317): --ceiling USD means stop before the next step once the limit is reached (the default mode); --ceiling USD --finish-item means the item in progress finishes first; --no-ceiling means no cap, chosen explicitly. With none of these, with --finish-item but no --ceiling, or with a USD that is not a positive number, the loop refuses to start as a usage error (exit 2) and nothing changes.

Each refusal names what to do instead and changes nothing: no item given; an unknown item id; a closed item (done or dropped); the same item twice; a loop already on (names vbw loop stop); the current milestone still has requirements and is not shipped (says to finish or ship it first, since each item gets its own milestone); --ceiling when no session has a cost figure (says vbw statusline on, or --no-ceiling), because a limit VBW cannot measure is no limit.

vbw loop stop, run from the session that started the loop or from any other session of the project, marks the loop as stopping with the time and the session, and vbw loop status then says so; stop with no loop on says so and exits 0; a second stop changes nothing. The loop state file is read, never guessed from a session file, so the stop is seen by the session running the loop before its next step.

Delegated approval: when a loop is on and not stopping, and vbw next would ask for approval, and the current milestone's requirements are exactly loop items (every requirement's text equals the recorded text of one loop item, each item matches at most once, and no other requirement is in the milestone, except a [human] requirement an earlier ship carried over for the user to judge), the kernel approves the contract with no question: consent is granted for the contract's fingerprint, the shape and the approved-contract snapshot are written exactly as vbw approve writes them, the project commands and the test-file form are approved too (D315), a decision is recorded whose text says the contract was approved by the loop on the user's behalf and names the loop's start time, the items and the fingerprint, and the approval commit is made. vbw next then moves past approve.

Any other contract waits for the user exactly as today: a requirement whose text differs from its item's recorded text by one character; an extra requirement in the milestone; a requirement that matches an item not on this loop's list; no loop on; a loop that is stopping; a contract that is not ready (a missing check file, spec and record differing). phases.goal: /vbw:loop takes the loop's items in order through milestone, plan, approval by delegation, build, prove, fix, QA and ship without asking anyone, and stops at the cost ceiling, at the end of its list or on a stop from any session, leaving .vbw/loop-report.md.

One kernel command (recommended: vbw loop next --json) does every step that needs no agent and returns the first that does. For the next waiting item it opens a milestone titled with the item (vbw milestone start, or the current milestone renamed when it has no requirements), adds the item's recorded text as that milestone's one requirement ([auto] unless only a person can judge it, then [human]), and marks the item in progress; it approves by delegation (P127) when vbw next says approve; it runs vbw ship when vbw next says ship, also when skipped [human] requirements are all that is left (ship now, judge later: D256); it marks a shipped item's backlog entry done; it answers done when the list is finished and stopped with the reason otherwise. Steps that need an agent (plan, build, fix, qa) or a proof come back as vbw next gives them, with the same detail, rigor, effort and profile fields the router passes to workflows. vbw next itself stays a pure reading of the record.

The Stop hook gate drives the cycle in the loop's own session: while a loop is on in this session, the gate blocks the stop with the next loop step (as the autonomous gate does today), never counts the loop's steps against settings.autonomy_cap (the ceiling is the loop's cap), asks for nothing while this session's proof or workflow still runs in the background, and lets the session stop once the loop reports done or stopped. In any other session the gate ignores the loop. The loop's steps are the ones the /vbw:vibe router describes for each action, run the same way (same workflows, same arguments).

A [human] requirement at the accept step is skipped by the loop (vbw req skip), never accepted or rejected on the user's behalf; the ship moves it to the next milestone, and the report lists it as waiting for the user's judgment.

A decision that planning asks for (needs_decisions) is taken with the recommended option and recorded with vbw decide as chosen by the loop with the trade-off accepted; the guided autonomy setting never makes the loop ask; the loop accepts no suggestion (R40) on the user's behalf.

Stops. Default ceiling: before each step the loop compares its spend with the ceiling; at or above it, or when the spend cannot be told, the loop stops before that step with that reason (a workflow or proof already running is never killed; the loop stops once it has returned and its result is recorded). --finish-item: once reached, the current item runs on to its ship (or its park, P129) and then the loop stops. --no-ceiling: no comparison. End of list: the loop stops after the last item's ship. vbw loop stop from any session: the loop stops before its next step with the reason stopped by the user and the session that asked.

Anything the loop cannot do without the user stops the loop in this phase with the reason, the item and the step (an escalated fix, a blocked plan, a scope violation, an action the loop does not know); P129 replaces this with retry and park. phases.title: Retry once, then park; nothing leaves the project
phases.goal: An item whose fix escalates is retried once and then set aside cleanly so the loop moves on with the project back at its last proven state, and nothing the loop does can push, release or publish.
criteria: At the escalate step, the first time for an item, the loop runs vbw fix retry for each escalated fix and continues (the fix workflow runs again); the loop state records the retry against the item. A blocked plan is likewise reset once (vbw plan reset) for a second attempt.

A second escalation of the same item, a plan blocked again, or a scope violation parks the item through one kernel command (vbw loop park, callable only by the loop step, denied to agents): it reverts the item's commits made since its milestone began with git revert commits (history kept, nothing rewritten, no git reset --hard, no git clean; a file the user staged or edited by hand is left as it is); removes the item's requirement, phases, plans, checks, rules and fixes from the record and its line from .vbw/spec.md, so the next proof and the next approval are not held up by parked work; marks the milestone parked with the reason and freezes its cost as a ship does; records a decision naming the item, the reason, the revert commits and how to bring the work back (revert the reverts, or run the item again); leaves the item's backlog entry open; commits the record; then the loop starts the next item.

After a park the project proves as before the item started: on a fixture, vbw prove passes the checks that passed before the item, vbw next offers the next milestone (a parked milestone is left behind like a shipped one), vbw status and vbw show roadmap show the milestone as parked with its reason, and the record stays valid (no requirement without a milestone, no check whose file is gone).

phases.title: Runs take turns: one shared limit per computer
phases.goal: However many VBW projects, sessions and runs prove at once on one computer, VBW never runs more checks at the same time than about three quarters of its processor cores, and a run that finds the limit reached waits its turn, then gets the same results it would have got alone.
criteria: R181: the machine limit is three quarters of the processor cores, rounded down, at least 1 and at most 64, from the same core count check_jobs already uses (vbw_cores); when the core count cannot be read the limit is 1. There is no setting for it (D341).

R181: the shared slot store lives in <claude-config-dir>/vbw/ (CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR if set, else ~/.config/claude-code when that folder exists, else ~/.claude: the same order as tools/resolve-claude-dir.sh, read by one kernel function that the status line's settings lookup also uses). Nothing else is written outside the project.

R181: every unit that vbw prove, vbw fix done and vbw check run (a check, a project command such as the full test command, a test file) takes one slot from the shared store for exactly as long as its command runs, and gives it back when the command ends, passes, fails or times out (D340: one slot per unit, whatever it does inside).

R181: with a faked core count of 4 (limit 3), two projects each proving 6 units at once, plus a vbw fix done in one of them, never have more than 3 unit commands running at the same moment across all of them (each unit's command logs its start and end with a timestamp to a file the test owns, and the overlap is counted from that log).

R181: check_jobs stays a per-run cap below the machine limit: a run with check_jobs 2 never runs more than 2 units at once even when slots are free; a check_jobs above the machine limit never lifts a run above the machine limit.

R181: a check marked alone keeps its per-project meaning (R45: nothing else of the same project runs beside it) and takes one machine slot like any unit; a unit waits for its project's gate before it asks for a machine slot and never holds a machine slot while it waits for anything else, so two projects can never block each other forever (a test runs an alone check in one project and shared checks in another at limit 1 and both finish).

R181: equal turns (D339): when a slot frees and several runs wait, it goes to the waiting run that holds the fewest slots; between runs holding the same number, to the one that has waited longest. Test: limit 3, run A queued with 6 units holds 3, run B starts with 1 unit; B's unit starts before A's fourth unit.

R181: waiting changes no result: a unit's timeout counts from when its command starts, never from when it began waiting; a unit that waited reports pass, fail, exit code and output exactly as it would alone, and never fails, times out or is skipped because it waited.

R181: slots of a run that is gone are given back: a run killed outright (its process no longer exists) leaves slots that the next run to look at the store takes over; a run interrupted with Ctrl-C gives back its slots at once (the existing exit guard). The short lock that makes looking and taking one step is taken over when its owner process is gone, as the project gate's lock is today.

R181: when the store cannot be created, read or written (a read-only folder, or the Claude Code sandbox refusing writes outside the project), the proof, fix done or check still runs to the end with only check_jobs as its cap, its results are unaffected, and its output says once, in one plain line, that the computer-wide limit was not in force and why. A damaged store file is treated the same way and never stops a proof.

R181: tests set CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR to a folder inside the test's own directory; no test reads or writes the host's real Claude config folder. The suite passes under macOS /bin/bash 3.2 and bash 5 (no wait -n, no associative arrays), and every kernel and standards rule in tests/standards.bats still passes.

phases.title: One fix done per fix round
phases.goal: A fix round with several groups of fixes runs VBW's "did this break finished work" check (vbw fix done) once, for all the round's fixes together, after every Dev has returned. The round no longer runs several overlapping copies at once, and before/after measurements show what changed.
criteria: Before any change, a measurement is recorded as a decision. It names the fixture. On that fixture, one fix round with three groups of fixes, where each Dev runs its own vbw fix done, gives the wall-clock minutes, the number of checks and test files run, and how many of those ran more than once across groups.

After the change, the same fixture and round are measured again and recorded in the same decision: the wall-clock minutes, the checks and test files run, and the count that ran more than once, which is 0.

The decision names the chosen approach (one vbw fix done per round, run by the workflow after all Devs return) and the rejected one (a kernel lock that makes fix done runs wait for each other in one clone), each with its reason based on the measurement.

With N groups (N of 1 or more), the fixing workflow runs vbw fix done exactly once per round, after every Dev has returned. It names every fix whose Dev reported done. In a stubbed workflow run with three groups, the prompts contain exactly one instruction to run vbw fix done, and it lists all done fixes.

No Dev runs vbw fix done. The Dev fix prompt and plugin/agents/dev.md tell the Dev to commit its fix and check it with vbw check on its own fixes' checks only, never the whole test command or vbw fix done. The workflow then records the result.
A fix whose Dev reported blocked, or stopped before reporting, is left out of the round's vbw fix done. It stays open, and the workflow result names it with its status.

Each fix in the shared vbw fix done still ends as it would on its own. A fix with uncommitted changes, one whose files serve a failing check of finished work, or a test-command fix whose test files still fail stays open and is named with its reason. The other fixes close, and the workflow result says which fixes closed and which stayed open.
When the round has no session (args.session missing), the one vbw fix done still runs before the workflow returns.

If the agent running the round's vbw fix done stops or reports a failure, the workflow log prints the exact command to run by hand (vbw fix done followed by the fix ids). The round is not reported complete.
A vbw fix done that runs longer than one shell command's time limit in Claude Code (10 minutes) still runs to the end, and its result is read before the run is confirmed and ended.

Afterwards, vbw run confirm counts every closed fix as recorded and names every fix still open. The router's vbw prove after the round runs as before and reuses the results the round's vbw fix done saved.
The output of vbw fix done is unchanged: one line per check or test file, then both count lines.

docs/workflows.md (the vbw:fixing row, the vbw fix done row and the run-closing text) and plugin/agents/dev.md describe the new order. The workflows stay within their 1,500-line JavaScript budget, and all prompts stay within their word budget.

phases.title: Leftover proof copies are cleaned up
phases.goal: When a VBW proof is killed outright, the full project copy it was checking in (under .vbw/runtime/proof.*) no longer stays on disk: the next vbw prove or vbw fix done removes every copy whose owning process has ended, and never one still in use.
criteria: Every proof copy records which process owns it (its process id, or pid) when it is created and before anything is copied into it, so no copy exists without an owner for longer than that first step. Example: the pid goes in the copy folder's name (proof.PID.XXXXXX, made in one step by mktemp) or in a file inside the folder, as the gate's mutex/pid does.

Before it makes its own copies, vbw prove removes every .vbw/runtime/proof.* copy whose owner process is no longer running (checked with kill -0, as checks_gate_live does). The same happens in vbw fix done, because both make copies through the same proofcopy code path.

A copy whose owner process is still running is never removed or changed, even when another vbw prove or vbw fix done in the same clone is cleaning up at the same moment. Test: start a live process, give it a copy, run a proof, and the copy is still whole afterwards.

Removing a dead copy also deletes its git worktree entry: afterwards `git worktree list` does not show it and .git/worktrees has no entry for it. Read-only folders inside the copy are removed too, and the removal never follows a link out of the copy.

An older copy with no owner recorded (made by a VBW version before this change, like the 13 MB one seen on 2026-10-12) is removed when it is more than 24 hours old, and kept when it is newer, because it might belong to a run of an older VBW still going.

Two cleanups running at once, or a cleanup killed partway through, never make a proof fail or print an error. A copy already removed by someone else is skipped, and a half-removed copy is finished by the next proof.
If a dead copy cannot be removed (for example, a file there cannot be deleted), the proof still runs and gives the same result. A one-line warning names the folder that is left.
The proof's result (pass or fail, and which checks ran) is the same with and without leftover copies present.

A bats test (hermetic, using tests/helper.bash) kills a proof with kill -9 after its copy exists, then runs the next proof. It shows the dead copy and its worktree entry are gone, and a live process's copy is still there. Run without the fix, the test fails.
docs/proof.md says that copies record their owner and that the next proof removes copies left by a process that has ended.
Bash 3.2 rules hold, the kernel stays within its 7,600-line budget, and bash tools/test.sh passes under /bin/bash.

phases.title: VBW stays out of sight in projects where it is turned off
phases.goal: In a project where the user turned the VBW plugin off, Claude Code's status line (the lines at the bottom of the screen) and the VBW panel show nothing from VBW: the user sees their own earlier status line, or none, as if VBW had never been installed there.
criteria: In a project whose .claude/settings.json (the project's own Claude Code settings file) sets enabledPlugins "vbw@vbw-marketplace" to false, and the user had no status line before VBW's, the status line shows nothing: no VBW lines and no '[VBW] status line unavailable' message.

In the same project, when the user had their own status line before VBW replaced it (the one VBW saved at 'vbw statusline on'), that status line shows instead, receiving the same information Claude Code sends to a status line (its JSON input), so it looks exactly as it did before VBW was installed.

VBW's own status line script never runs the saved status line command itself (decision D356, rule: no command read from a file is run by VBW); the command Claude Code runs from the user's settings is what hands over to the saved one. A test shows the saved command text is never executed by vbw-statusline.sh.

The on/off answer follows Claude Code's own order of settings files: .claude/settings.local.json in the project wins over .claude/settings.json in the project, which wins over the user's own settings.json. So: project file says false -> hidden; user file says false and the project says nothing -> hidden; user file says false but the project says true -> VBW shows; local file says true over a project false -> VBW shows. Each case has a test.
The project's settings are read from the same project folder the status line already uses (the folder Claude Code reports, or the nearest folder up holding .git when started in a subfolder).

Nothing changes when no setting turns VBW off: missing settings files, an enabledPlugins entry that is absent, another plugin turned off, or a settings file that is not valid JSON all leave the VBW status line showing its usual four lines, and the script still never fails.

In a project where VBW is on, the status line output is byte-for-byte what it was before this change, and the session's cost file (.vbw/runtime/cost.SESSION.json) is still written; in a project where VBW is off, the status line writes no file anywhere in the project.

Users who turned VBW's status line on before this change get the new behaviour without editing anything by hand: 'vbw statusline on' (also run by /vbw:init) updates the setting in place, keeps the user's refresh interval and the saved earlier status line, and 'vbw doctor' flags an older setting with 'vbw statusline on' as the fix.
'vbw statusline status' still reports 'on' for the updated setting, and 'vbw statusline off' still restores the user's earlier status line exactly (or removes VBW's when there was none), as today.

Speed: the status line stays within its 60 ms limit in a project where VBW is on, and the hand-back in a project where VBW is off is measured by a speed check with the same limit; a machine too busy to measure is reported as busy, not failed (R151).

The panel (VBW's live view, loaded by Claude Code from the plugin's hooks.json module list): whether Claude Code loads it in a project where the plugin is off is checked in a real Claude Code session and the result is recorded with its evidence; if it does show there, it shows nothing in that project, with a test; if it does not, no panel code changes.

docs/statusline.md explains, in plain words, what the status line shows in a project where VBW is turned off and how the user's earlier status line comes back there; docs/panel.md does the same if the panel changed.

phases.title: The config skill names the computer-wide limit beside check_jobs
VBW records proof that a plan's tests can fail, and will not finish the plan without it
phases.goal: At standard and deep, VBW itself runs a plan's tests against deliberately broken code, records whether they failed, and refuses to mark the plan done until every promised behaviour has been shown to be caught (a "mutation check": break the code on purpose and confirm the tests notice).
criteria: A new vbw subcommand runs the checks of one approved rule (standard) or one plan task (deep) against code a Dev has deliberately broken, and writes the result to the record under that plan: the rule or task, a one-line description of what was broken, the checks run, and whether each failed (red) or still passed (green).

The command refuses, writing nothing, when: nothing differs from the plan's last commit (no break applied); the break touches a file outside the plan's files; the break touches any check file; or the same checks do not pass on the unbroken code (a test already failing proves nothing).

A break that leaves every one of the rule's checks passing is recorded as a survivor (a test that cannot fail) and named in the command's output with the rule it belongs to; the command exits non-zero.
While one Dev's break is being checked, another Dev of the same wave running vbw check on its own checks gets the same result as with no break applied (breaks never leak into parallel work).
After a mutation check the plan's files are byte-identical to their last commit; vbw plan done refuses while they are not, naming the files.

At standard, vbw plan done refuses until every approved rule of each requirement this plan completes (no other open plan serves it, the same rule plan done already uses for checks) has a recorded break whose checks went red; the refusal lists the rules still missing one. Rules that share one check each need their own break.

At deep, vbw plan done additionally refuses until every task of the plan has a recorded red break, or is marked as having no testable behaviour with a written reason (for example a task that only runs a script); the reason is shown in vbw show plan.
At express, and for plans whose requirements are all [human] (no checks), vbw plan done behaves exactly as before: no mutation check is asked for.
A survivor whose check file was then changed and re-checked red counts as covered; vbw show plan lists each break, its result, and which check files were strengthened.
Mutation-check runs take machine slots like any other check run (the computer-wide limit and check_jobs still hold).
Every new kernel path is bash 3.2 compatible, passes JSON only through jq, and keeps the kernel within its 7,600-line budget; each behaviour above has a bats test shown to fail before the code.

phases.title: VBW knows what each long step is doing and when it should end
phases.goal: While planning, a build, a fix, a proof or QA runs, VBW's kernel (its record-keeping core) keeps one up-to-date note of what the step is doing, how far along it is and the clock time it should end, worked out from how long the same kind of step took before in this project.
criteria: When a step ends, VBW adds it to the step history (steps.json in the project's git folder, private to this computer): its kind (plan, build, fix, qa, map or proof), start, end, seconds and, where it has countable parts, how many: plans for build and fix, checks and test files actually run for a proof.

A proof (vbw prove, and the proof inside vbw fix done) is recorded as a step of kind proof. A proof that reused every earlier result and ran nothing is not recorded, so it never teaches VBW a false zero.

The history keeps the latest 50 steps of each kind, so many proofs never push out the planning or QA history. A missing, damaged or unwritable history file never fails a step: it means 'no end time yet'.

Expected length: for a kind with parts, the median time per part over its latest 10 finished steps that recorded parts, times this step's number of parts. For a kind without parts (planning, QA, map), the median of its latest 10 finished steps. With fewer than 3 finished steps of that kind there is no end time, never a guess.

While a step runs, vbw status --json and one note under .vbw/runtime/ (written only by the kernel) give: the kind, what it is doing now (the plan ids building, 'check 12 of 40', the phase QA is checking), parts done of total, start time, first end time, current end time, and whether it is later than usual, or that there is no basis yet.

Parts done update within 2 seconds of each vbw plan done in a build or fix and of each finished proof unit. With the proof running checks in 4 parallel lanes, 40 finished units read exactly 40 of 40, never fewer or more (a test proves it).
A proof that runs inside a build or fix shows as what that step is doing now ('proving 12 of 40 checks'); the end time stays the build's or fix's.

Late step with parts (D424): once this run's own pace (time so far divided by parts done, times parts left) puts the end after the first end time, the current end time moves to that projection and is marked later than usual. It can move again. It never moves earlier than the first end time.
Late step without parts (D424): the end time stays the first one, and the note says how many minutes past it the step is.

A note whose run has ended, or whose proof process is gone (killed outright), is ignored and removed by the next step or proof; it never shows a step as running. A proof of another session never replaces this session's own step.
The kernel rules hold: bash 3.2, JSON only through jq, nothing written outside the project except the clone's git folder; the Stop hook still waits while a background proof runs.

phases.title: A step's end time comes from the time per unit of work at its rigor tier, times the work's size
phases.goal: When VBW starts planning, a build, a fix, a proof or QA, the end time it gives is worked out from how long one unit of that work (a plan's task at its rigor tier, a proof's check, a phase at its tier, a requirement) took before in this project, multiplied by the size of this step, instead of one average per kind of step.
criteria: The step history (steps.json in the project's git folder, the private file where VBW keeps how long past steps took) records, for every finished step, its units: a build records each plan with its id, its rigor tier (express, standard or deep, taken from the plan's phase at that moment), its number of tasks and its own seconds (from the run's start to that plan's vbw plan done); a fix round records its fixes and the highest tier of their phases; a proof records every unit it ran (check, test file or command) with that unit's own seconds; planning records the number of open requirements it planned; QA records the phases it checked with each phase's tier. Entries written before this change (kind, seconds, parts only) stay readable and are still counted at the coarse level below.

A plan's expected seconds are the median seconds per task over the latest 10 finished plans of the same tier in the history, times this plan's tasks. With fewer than 3 finished plans of that tier with tasks, VBW falls back to the median seconds per plan at that tier; with fewer than 3 of those, to the median per plan of any tier (today's rule); with fewer than 3 plans in all, there is no end time. A test shows each rung of this ladder being used, and that a guess is never shown when the bottom rung lacks 3 plans.

A build wave's expected time is the longest expected time among its plans (they build side by side), never their sum; a test with two plans of different sizes shows the wave's time equals the bigger plan's. A fix round's expected time is the median wall time of the latest 10 fix rounds whose tier matches (else any tier; fewer than 3 in all gives no time): the round's Devs work side by side and end with one shared vbw fix done, so its time does not grow with the fix count.

A proof's expected time is the sum of its units' own last recorded seconds (from runs.json, the per-check store in the project's git folder; a unit never run before counts as the median of the known ones), multiplied by the median ratio of wall time to summed unit time over the latest 10 proofs (so parallel lanes and this machine's load are learned, not assumed). With fewer than 3 finished proofs there is no time. A test with 4 units of known seconds and a seeded ratio shows the expected seconds equal the sum times the ratio, rounded.

Planning's expected time is the median seconds per open requirement over the latest 10 planning steps that recorded a count, times the requirements to plan now (fewer than 3 such steps: the median planning time, as today). QA's expected time is the sum, over the phases it will check, of the median seconds per phase at that phase's tier (fewer than 3 at a tier: per phase of any tier; fewer than 3 in all: no time).

vbw next --json's step, the running step's note (.vbw/runtime/step.json) and vbw run start's sentence all use these expected times; the wording of D425 ('about 12 min, until around 14:20', 'later than usual', 'N min late', 'no end time yet') is unchanged, so the status line, Comms and Mission Control need no change for the step's time. The history keeps the latest 50 steps of each kind; a missing, damaged or unwritable history or runs store never fails a step and only means 'no end time yet'. The kernel rules hold: bash 3.2, JSON only through jq, record-sized data never on a command line, nothing written outside the project except the project's git folder (D433: no computer-wide pool).

phases.title: VBW works out when the whole milestone should end, counting the usual fix rounds
phases.goal: The kernel (VBW's record-keeping core) gives one clock time for the end of the milestone, adding up everything still ahead on the road (planning, each build wave, each proof, QA and the fix rounds a phase of that rigor tier usually needs in this project), and names the assumption it made.
criteria: vbw next --json carries road (null when there is no milestone or nothing is left): {seconds, end, rounds: {tier: n, ...}, basis, say}. end is the UTC time the milestone should end; say is the one sentence VBW uses everywhere, for example 'Milestone end: about 2 h 10 min, until around 16:40, counting 2 fix rounds per deep phase (the usual here)'. The same road is in vbw status --json and printed by vbw status and /vbw:status under the running step's line.

The road adds, for every phase of the milestone not yet passed by QA: the expected time of each build wave still to build (P149's rule, from the plans' tiers and tasks, waves as vbw show contract lists them); one proof per wave sized by the phase's checks and test files not yet passed (P149's proof rule); QA when the phase's tier needs it (the same needs_qa rule vbw next uses); and the phase's usual fix rounds, each counted as one fix round plus one proof plus one QA recheck (medians of P149). A running step contributes its current end time (moved when late), not its first estimate.

Usual fix rounds per tier are the median of outcome.fix_rounds over the latest 10 finished phases of that tier in this project's record, rounded to a whole number; with fewer than 3 finished phases of that tier the road counts 0 rounds and the sentence says so ('counting no fix rounds: fewer than 3 finished deep phases here'). A test with seeded outcomes (deep: 1, 2, 2, 5 rounds) shows 2 counted; one with two deep outcomes shows 0 counted and the stated reason.

Before planning (the milestone has no phases yet) the road is the planning step alone and the sentence says the rest follows once the work is planned; it never guesses the unplanned work. When any needed piece has no basis (for example fewer than 3 proofs), road.end is null and say names the missing kind: 'no milestone end time yet (VBW has timed fewer than 3 proofs here)'. A made-up time never appears.

The road is written by the kernel next to the step: into .vbw/runtime/next.json by vbw next, and into the running step's note by vbw run start and at every vbw plan done or proof unit that moves the step's end, so a step running later than usual moves the milestone's end by the same amount within 2 seconds. Only the kernel writes these files.
With no phase left (the milestone is ready to ship or shipped) road is null and nothing is shown; the first vbw next of a new milestone gives a road again.

Clock times follow the step's rules (local 24-hour HH:MM, 'tomorrow 00:20' on another day); durations over an hour read 'about 2 h 10 min'. A test with one fixed history shows vbw next --json, vbw status --json and the note give the identical end time.

Bash 3.2, JSON only through jq, record-sized data by pipe or file (never --arg), and vbw next stays within its current test's time budget on the 2 MB record used by tests/big-record tests (the road is computed once per vbw next, not per phase per call).

Which run is judged, and from where: the kernel reads the check's last recorded run from the clone's run store (`vbw/runs.json` in the git directory, where `vbw prove` and `vbw fix done` keep each unit's read list) and uses it only while it is current: the check's approved definition is unchanged and, between the tree it ran on and the committed code, no file on its read list changed or was deleted and no listed folder's listing changed (the proof's own reuse rule, applied whatever the run's pass or fail). phases.title: A commit exactly undone by a later commit is not judged by the scope check
phases.goal: A proof no longer fails because of a commit (a saved change) that a later commit on the branch put back exactly, whoever made that later commit and whether or not it says it is a revert; a partial or edited undo is still judged, and the proof says which commits it left unjudged and why.
criteria: What counts as an exact undo, verified with git and nothing else: a later commit B exactly undoes an earlier commit A when git shows that A is an ancestor of B (A comes before B on the branch that leads to the current HEAD), that both change exactly the same set of file paths, and that for every path B's change is the mirror image of A's as git lists them (`git log --raw --no-abbrev --no-renames`: A takes the path from old mode and old blob id to new mode and new blob id; B takes it from A's new pair back to A's old pair; a file A added is deleted by B, a file A deleted is added back by B with the same content and mode, a mode-only change is put back). A blob id is git's fingerprint of a file's exact content, so an edited revert (one extra or missing line, a whitespace change, a different mode), a partial revert (one path of two restored, or an extra path touched) or a revert made from a commit message alone is not exact and the earlier commit is judged as today. No commit message, trailer or author is read for this: a hand-made `git revert`, a revert by the loop's park, a revert made with any other tool and a commit that happens to restore the same content all count the same.

Which commits are left unjudged: in the proof's scope check (the step that confirms every commit naming a plan of the current milestone changed only that plan's files), a commit with a `VBW-Plan:` trailer naming a plan of the current milestone is not judged when a standing later commit exactly undoes it; the undoing commit itself, when it carries such a trailer, is not judged either, since the pair leaves every file as it was. A later commit stands only while it is not itself exactly undone by a later standing commit, and each standing commit clears at most one commit: the nearest earlier one it is the mirror image of. So: an undo that is itself undone (revert of a revert, `Reapply`) clears nothing and the original is judged again; a re-apply made after a revert is a fresh commit, judged on its own when it carries a trailer; a chain of apply, undo, apply, undo leaves all four unjudged. A park's recorded reverts (`.loop.items[].reverts`, T163) keep clearing their originals as today, since a park's revert that git had to merge over a later change is not exact at the file level. Everything not covered here is judged exactly as today (a shipped milestone's commits are not judged, every other commit of the current milestone's plans is).

The proof reports what it skipped, in the record and on screen: the evidence gains `evidence.undone`, an array of `{commit, plan, by}` (the 40-hex id of the unjudged commit, the plan its trailer names, the 40-hex id of the commit that undid it), one entry per cleared commit whose trailer names a plan of the current milestone (an undoing commit left unjudged because of its own trailer is listed with itself as `commit` and its original as `by`), `[]` when none. The proof's summary prints, after its scope line, one line per entry `scope: abc123456789 (P163.2) undone by def123456789, not judged` (12-character ids), and `vbw show evidence` prints the same lines; a record written before this field still reads and both print nothing for it. The record validator accepts the field and refuses an entry missing `commit`, `plan` or `by`, with a non-40-hex id, or with a plan id of a wrong shape; `evidence.passed` and the `scope[]` violations keep their meaning and shape, `vbw next --json`'s `scope` action and the loop's park on a scope violation are unchanged, and the contract fingerprint is untouched.

The scope check costs a fixed number of git processes however long the history is: one `git log --topo-order --no-renames --raw --no-abbrev -z` walk (with the `VBW-Plan` trailer in its format) replaces today's walk plus one `git diff-tree` per trailer commit (1,255 such commits on this repository; 500 of them took 8.4 s on this Mac), plus at most one ancestry check (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`) per undone pair found; a test counts the git processes of a proof on a history with 5 plan-trailer commits and one with 50, with no undone pair, and finds the same number. The violations found, their wording and their order are exactly today's for every commit not cleared (the existing scope tests in tests/kernel-prove.bats, tests/scope-shipped.bats and tests/park-ids.bats stay green except the one test the next criterion rewrites). The walk uses `-z` for paths, parses nothing with grep or sed on JSON, and builds the per-commit pairs without reading any file content.

Tests, each shown red before its code, in a new test file and in tests/park-ids.bats: the T169 shape (five commits naming a current plan and touching a file outside it, reverted newest first by hand with `git revert`, no park: the proof passes, `scope ok`, five `undone` entries, five summary lines); the same with the reverts made as plain commits that restore the content without any `This reverts commit` line (still cleared); an undo with one extra line (judged, the violation names the file); an undo that restores one of two files (judged); a mode-only change and its exact undo (cleared); a file added then deleted again (cleared); a revert made before the original, that is, a re-apply after a revert (the re-apply is judged, the first commit is judged again); a revert of a revert (the original is judged again); a park's revert that merged over a later edit of the same file (still cleared through the park's list); the existing test `a commit undone by hand, not by a park, is still judged` becomes `a commit undone by hand with an edit is still judged` (its revert gains one extra change) and a sibling test pins that an exact hand revert is no longer judged; the validator's accept and refuse cases; a record without `undone` read by `vbw show evidence`; the process-count test. criteria: The spec gains a section '## Clean copy' with one path per line ('- data/'), relative to the project root; vbw init's starting spec.md explains it in the same comment style as the other sections; a spec without the section behaves exactly as today (nothing left out).

vbw spec sync copies the listed paths into the record under one field validated by record.jq (a record without the field still validates, so older projects open unchanged); 'vbw spec check' and 'vbw spec sync' refuse a listed path that git does not ignore (tracked, or untracked but not ignored) or that does not exist, naming the spec line and the path and saying why ('is not git-ignored: only ignored paths are copied in, so only they can be left out' / 'does not exist'), and the record is left unchanged; an absolute path, a path with '..', or one under .vbw/ or .git/ is refused like a bad Test results folder.

The left-out paths are part of the contract: contract_core and contract_doc include them, so changing the list changes the fingerprint and the approval menu is asked again; 'vbw show contract' prints one line 'clean copy leaves out: data/, cache/' (absent when nothing is listed); 'vbw show contract --changes' names an added or removed path; vbw approve and vbw next compare this spec section with the record like the other sections (R174, R171): an edited, unsynced section cannot be approved and vbw next says the contract is not ready.

Every clean copy (vbw prove, vbw fix done, vbw mutate single form, --run and the one run of Rn.k --none) skips a listed path and everything under it: with two ignored folders and one listed, the copy holds the other one whole and nothing of the listed one, including when only files inside the listed path are ignored (git lists them one by one); build folders are left out as before; a listed path that no longer exists at copy time changes nothing (the next sync refuses it).

The proof's results do not change because a path was left out: the proof verdict, reuse decisions and read lists are the same with the list and without it for a project whose checks never read the left-out data.

docs/proof.md describes the section, the refusals, the contract line and that the copy skips the listed paths; a test file of the requirement area covers each rule above; a new real-user scenario in tools/l3-suite.sh ('leaveout': a project ignoring a data folder, listed in the spec, reaching an approved contract whose 'vbw show contract' names the path and a passed proof) runs and its result is saved under tools/l3-results/.
