phases.title: A big plain copy of ignored data is named with its size and the way out
phases.goal: When a proof or mutation run has to copy more than 500 MB of ignored data file by file (the disk offers no instant copy-on-write clone), the user is told which ignored folders cost the most and how to leave them out; a clone or a small copy says nothing.
criteria: proofcopy_copy records, per top-level ignored path it copied, whether the copy-on-write clone succeeded or the plain copy ran, and for a plain copy the size of what it copied, counted once per command (not once per copy slot) and within the 'copies' step of VBW's own work.

When the plain-copied data of one clean copy exceeds 500 MB, vbw prove, vbw fix done and vbw mutate (single form, --run, Rn.k --none) print exactly one line to stderr starting 'vbw:' naming the up to three largest ignored folders copied with their sizes (MB or GB, one decimal) and the way out ('list them under ## Clean copy in .vbw/spec.md, then vbw spec sync'); the line is printed once even when several copies are made.

Nothing is printed when every ignored path was cloned copy-on-write, when the plain-copied data is 500 MB or less, or when nothing ignored exists; the line never changes the command's verdict, evidence, record or exit code.

Tests force the plain-copy path (the clone refused) and the size threshold without creating 500 MB of real data (the size reader is injectable or measured on small files with a lowered threshold through a test-only variable), and show the line absent in the three silent cases; docs/proof.md names the threshold, the line and the way out beside the copy-on-write paragraph.

phases.title: VBW's own plan files are never hidden by the project's git ignore rules
phases.goal: A project whose .gitignore hides JSON or Markdown files still commits VBW's record, spec and map, and when a rule hides the whole .vbw folder (which nothing inside it can undo) VBW says so by name instead of committing nothing.
criteria: vbw init writes .vbw/.gitignore with 'runtime/' and the un-hide lines '!record.json', '!spec.md', '!map.md' and '!.gitignore' (the last so a project-wide '*' rule cannot hide the file itself), prints one line saying VBW keeps its plan files visible to git through .vbw/.gitignore, and in an already-initialized project adds only the missing lines, keeps every line the user added, and leaves the file byte-identical when run again.

Every VBW commit of its own files (record_commit: approval, run end, proof, ship, vbw todo, spec sync) first adds the missing un-hide lines to .vbw/.gitignore and commits that file along with the others, so an existing project gets them at its next VBW commit; with the lines present a record.json or spec.md that a project-wide '*.json' or '*.md' rule would hide is committed (shown with such a rule in the project's .gitignore, .git/info/exclude and a global excludes file).

When an own file that exists is untracked and still ignored after the un-hide lines (a rule such as '.vbw/' or '*' hiding the folder), vbw init prints the rule's source as 'git check-ignore -v' gives it (file, line number, pattern) with the fix ('remove that line, or change it to .vbw/runtime/'); vbw doctor prints the same as a fail line and exits 1; vbw approve refuses with that message, exit 1, adding no decision, granting no consent and making no commit; vbw next names it among the reasons the contract is not ready (R171) instead of offering the approval menu.

record_commit never skips a hidden own file silently: in its non-strict form it prints a 'vbw: warning:' line naming the file and the rule's source line; in strict form (vbw approve) the reason is the refusal above; a project with no such rule prints nothing new and commits as today.

docs (docs/proof.md or the page that documents vbw init and vbw doctor, plus docs/record.md where it lists VBW's own files) state the un-hide lines, the whole-folder case and the fix; a test file of the requirement area covers each rule above on both shells; the 'greenfield' real-user scenario is run again and a new scenario ('hiddenrecord': a project whose .gitignore holds '*.json', reaching an approved contract with .vbw/record.json committed) runs, both results saved under tools/l3-results/.

phases.title: vbw mutate ends with where its time went, step by step
phases.goal: A developer running a mutation check sees, at the end, how long VBW spent on each step (copies, the unbroken run, each break's checks, waits for a slot, saving) in the same shape the proof's time line uses, without any change to what the check decides.

WHAT FILE... and vbw mutate PLAN --run end with a line in the proof's form ('VBW's own work: X of Y min', minutes with one decimal, measured by prooftime.sh's clock, nothing estimated) followed by the split by step: copies (making, checking and removing the clean copies), unbroken (the checks on the unbroken code), one entry per break named by its target ('break R3.1'), waits (seconds spent waiting for a computer-wide slot, the figure slots already count), saving (recording the result); the steps sum to the wall time within rounding.

phases.title: A weak test in a shared test file can be made stronger
phases.goal: When VBW's mutation step (it breaks the code on purpose to see whether a test notices) finds a test that cannot fail, the Dev can strengthen that test even when its file also holds other requirements' tests, the user sees the whole change before approving it, and the same break then turns the test red.
criteria: The kernel has one definition (in the shared jq defs of plugin/lib/record.sh, beside own_rules) of the check files a plan may strengthen: the files of the checks named by the plan's own rules (own_rules), opened once a survivor is recorded in that plan's build run. vbw commit PLAN, the build lease's editable list written by vbw mutate, the file guard (plugin/hooks/common.jq), the proof's scope check (PROVE_SCOPE_JQ and PROVE_SCOPE_THEN_JQ in cmd-prove.sh) and the pending/strengthened logic of mutate_record all read that one definition; COMMIT_SURVIVOR_DEFS in cmd-commit.sh no longer holds a second one.

Given a check file that holds C1 (a check of one of the plan's own rules) and C2 (a check of another requirement, or of another plan's rule), after vbw mutate records a survivor of the plan's rule: vbw commit PLAN MSG FILE commits the file with the plan's VBW-Plan and VBW-Req trailers, and the file guard lets the Dev write it during the build run. Before any survivor of that plan, the guard and vbw commit refuse the file as today.

A check file that no check of the plan's own rules names (one listed only by other requirements' checks or other plans' rules' checks) is still refused by vbw commit, naming the file, with a message that states the new rule (the current wording 'no other requirement's check file is the plan's to commit' is replaced); the refusal ends with the next step. A plan with no recorded survivor is refused as today.

The strengthened file waits for the user's approval before the proof as any check edit: after the build finishes, vbw next asks to approve the edited file by name, vbw prove refuses until it is approved, and under a loop the loop approves and records a decision naming the file (existing behaviour, still held by tests).

The whole diff is shown at the approval: vbw show contract --changes prints, under each 'changed test file F' line, the complete difference between the content the approval covered and the file as it is now (committed or not), every hunk included, so the user sees that other requirements' cases in the same file were not weakened; when the approved content cannot be found in the project's git history, it says so in one line instead of printing nothing or a wrong diff. The router's approve step (plugin/skills/vibe/SKILL.md) shows that diff to the user before the approval question.

The survivor can be re-run: after the commit, vbw mutate PLAN Rn.k with the same break runs the strengthened file and prints 'TARGET survives the approved check; caught by the pending one: F', exits 0, records the break as red with pending [F] and strengthened [F], and says the pending file still needs the one approval before the proof.

vbw prove's scope check counts the commit of the shared check file as the plan's: no 'changed F, which is not in the plan' violation, judged by the record version of the commit's time as for a plan's own files.

Docs and prompts say the new rule in the same words: plugin/agents/dev.md step 4 (survivor line) and DEVN-04, docs/proof.md's mutation-check survivor paragraph and the vbw commit section, docs/record.md's lease editable description. criteria: R215 refusal: in every mode (full apply, --add, --patch), judged on the record as the document would leave it, when a check's live (not retired) rules name two different plans A and B of the current milestone and neither is done (a blocked plan counts as not done), vbw apply refuses before anything changes, naming the check and both plans, prefixed with the mode's name (R156) and ending with a Next line; the record is unchanged, shown by a byte comparison in the test.

R215 words: when B builds after A (A in B's after directly or through a chain, A's and B's files overlap under the wave rule of record.sh, or A's wave comes before B's in waves($m) on the merged record judged as if no plan were blocked), the message keeps R211's words exactly as today ('C is owned by two plans that build one after the other (WHY): A and B; the earlier plan's mutation step would find C red on unbroken code'), WHY being 'B builds after A', 'A and B share a file' or the new 'A builds in an earlier wave than B'; when neither builds after the other and they would share a wave, the message reads 'C is owned by two plans that build beside each other (a shared wave): A and B; the first Dev's mutation step would run C before the other Dev committed, a race that fails only sometimes'. The test asserts each wording on its own fixture.

R215 edges: the R211 non-refusals stay (all rules naming one plan, no rule naming a plan, one of the two plans done, the check of another milestone's requirement, a retired rule counting for nothing); the 'plans build beside each other' acceptance in tests/apply-refusal-modes.bats (the R211 no-refusal case) is edited into a refusal asserting the beside words, not stacked; a pair in which one plan is blocked is refused like any open pair.

R216 pinned Next lines: apply_next answers both two-owner messages (ordered and beside) with one arm and the mixed-owner message (R212) with its arm; the R211, R215 and R212 cases in tests/apply-refusal-modes.bats assert the whole last line word for word: 'Next: give each plan's rules a check of their own (a separate test file, or the same file with a case filter as a distinct check), or move the rules to one plan' and 'Next: name a plan on every rule of the requirement, or on none (vbw apply --patch rewords a rule: {"rule": "Rn.k", "plan": "P1.1"})'; the next_line helper that only checks for a 'Next: ' prefix is no longer what those cases rely on.

R216 every refusal: every refusal message cmd-apply.sh builds itself (each literal apply_refuse message and each message string its jq filters produce, the R211/R215 and R212 ones included) is answered by an arm of its own in apply_next; the fallback arm answers only messages of the record's own validation (record_violation). tests/refusal-next-step.bats proves it: its apply_refusal helper (full, --add, --patch cases) also asserts the Next line differs from the fallback arm's text, the cases that are record validations (an unknown requirement, a plan for no phase) being named in the file as the ones that take the fallback by design; and one case feeds each two-owner and mixed-owner message to apply_next directly and fails on the fallback text, so a dropped arm turns the file red.

R216 docs: docs/workflows.md's 'Every refusal and its next step' table carries a row for the two-owner refusal (both wordings) and one for the mixed-owner refusal with the exact Next text above; a case in tests/rules-docs.bats pins each row's Next text to the kernel's words so the two cannot drift apart.

R215 in words: plugin/agents/lead.md rule 6 (Checks, test first) states that a check's rules belong to one plan and that when several open plans of a requirement would share a check, whatever their order and the same wave included, each plan's rules get a check of their own (a separate test file, or the same file with a case filter that is a distinct check), because vbw apply refuses a check whose rules two open plans own; the R211 case in tests/rules-prompts.bats that greps 'one after the other' is edited to the new words (not stacked). docs/proof.md's Rules bullet and docs/workflows.md's refusal list say the same (any two plans not yet built, order or not, naming the race for a shared wave); the R211 cases in tests/rules-docs.bats are edited to the new fact.

Tests first and lean: every case above is shown red before the code or text change and lives in the existing files of its area (tests/apply-refusal-modes.bats, tests/refusal-next-step.bats, tests/rules-prompts.bats, tests/rules-docs.bats); no new test file; tests/standards.bats stays green (bash 3.2, JSON only through jq, the record never on a command line).

phases.title: vbw mutate names pending and strengthened files from the one definition of what a plan may strengthen
phases.goal: When a break (the mutation step deliberately damaging the code to see whether a test notices) is recorded, the files vbw mutate calls 'pending' (edited and waiting for approval) and 'strengthened' are drawn only from the check files that plan may strengthen (strengthen_files, the one definition from R210), never from whatever check files the break happened to run, and the test file that pins R210 says exactly what its cases prove.
criteria: mutate_record (plugin/lib/cmd-mutate.sh) computes pending as the files of strengthen_files($p) (plugin/lib/record.sh's shared jq defs) that checks_begin listed as waiting for approval and that a check of this break that went red names; and strengthened as the files of strengthen_files($p) that differ between the prior survivor's head and HEAD. The files of the checks the break ran (cfiles, the red checks' files) are no longer a source of either list; the record is read through a pipe as today (tests/record-args-rule.bats green).

A check file outside strengthen_files($p) that the break ran (another requirement's check file, or another plan's rule's check file, edited and waiting for approval in the same build run) appears in neither pending nor strengthened, and the output is the plain red line, never 'caught by the pending one'; a shared file inside strengthen_files($p) that waits and whose check went red is pending and, after a prior survivor, strengthened, exactly as the R210 case of tests/mutate-strengthen.bats holds today (that case stays green).

Before any survivor is recorded in the plan, strengthen_files($p) is empty, so no file is pending or strengthened for a break of that plan whatever waits for approval; the R196 case 'a pending file with no earlier survivor of the target' in tests/mutate-pending-check.bats gets a survivor of another target of the same plan in its fixture (edited, not stacked); every other R196 case stays green unchanged.

The header of tests/mutate-strengthen.bats names only what the file's cases assert, each named reader (vbw commit, the lease's editable list, the file guard, the proof's scope check, vbw mutate's pending and strengthened lists) having a case in the file; the new case pinning that vbw mutate's pending and strengthened lists come from strengthen_files($p) (a waiting file of a check the break ran but the plan may not strengthen stays out of both) lives in that file and is shown red before the code change.

docs/proof.md's paragraph on 'caught by the pending one' and docs/record.md's mutations description say the pending and strengthened files are among the files the plan may strengthen (the files of its own rules' checks), pinned by one case in the docs test of the area (tests/mutate-pending-check-docs.bats), not a new file.

phases.title: The loop-writes rule sees a function that writes, not only a direct printf
phases.goal: The maintainer tool that forbids a builtin write (printf or echo) inside a loop fed by a process substitution (a shape where, on macOS bash 3.2, the written text can be lost) also refuses a call to a function whose body writes that way, finding those functions itself in the repository's shell files, while a function that writes safely (through vbw_out, a subshell, a pipeline or into a file) still passes.
criteria: tools/check-loop-writes.sh first collects, across every shell file under all the DIRs it is given (so a function defined in plugin/lib/core.sh is known when plugin/lib/cmd-doctor.sh calls it), the writer functions: a function whose body holds a builtin write that the tool's own rules judge to run in the function's shell (not in a command or process substitution, a subshell, a pipeline stage, a background job, a loop fed by a pipe, nor redirected into a file), and, to a fixed point, a function whose body calls a writer function under those same rules. vbw_out (printf in a subshell), vbw_die and vbw_usage_error (writing through vbw_out) are not writers; a function such as vbw_session (a bare printf) is.

Inside a loop fed by a process substitution, a call to a writer function in the loop's own shell is refused like a direct printf: FILE:LINE:text of the calling line, followed by the writer's name and where it writes (FILE:LINE), exit 1; a call in a command substitution, a subshell, a pipeline, the background, a loop fed by a pipe, or with its output redirected into a file passes, under the same redirection rules the tool applies to printf.

Self-test cases in tests/output-child-exit.bats, each shown red before the tool change: refused, named at the calling line, a planted writer called in such a loop; a writer defined in a second file under another DIR; a two-step chain (a calls b, b writes with echo >&2); passing, a function whose body writes through vbw_out, '( printf ... )', 'printf ... | cat' or 'printf ... > "$f"', and a writer called as '$(say x)', 'say x > file', 'say x | cat' or inside a pipe-fed loop; the existing vbw_die-in-a-loop acceptance stays as it is.

The shipped-code case (plugin/bin, lib, hooks, scripts) stays green on the widened rule; any call it newly refuses in shipped code is fixed in this phase in the way the rule prescribes (write through vbw_out or pipe the producer into the loop), with the fix named in the plan.

Wording: the tool's header replaces 'A function the body calls writes in the same shell and is not seen: such a call is the reviewer's to judge' with the writer-function rule; AGENTS.md's 'No builtin write while the shell has a live child' line says a call to a function that writes counts as the write (CLAUDE.md is a symlink to AGENTS.md, so one edit); the header of tests/output-child-exit.bats names the widened rule.

The tool stays bash 3.2 and awk only (no mapfile, no associative arrays; guarded array expansions under set -u), writes nothing outside the repository, and passes bash tools/test.sh --lint (shellcheck over tools/); tests/standards.bats stays green.

phases.title: The Bash guard stops a small inline program that writes a file it cannot name
phases.goal: While a builder or fixer works under a run, a short program typed straight into the command (Python, Node, Perl, Ruby and the other interpreters the guard already reads, given as a heredoc or a -c/-e argument) that writes a file but names that file through a variable, an expression or another call is stopped by the Bash guard, which says it cannot read where the program writes and names the fix (a literal path, or the Edit tool); a literal path is judged exactly as today, and a program that writes nothing still passes.
criteria: The rule, in plugin/hooks/guard-bash.jq: in every program text the guard reads today (the -c/-e and similar code arguments of a command whose cmd matches `interpreter`, and the body of a heredoc fed to one, `heredoc_programs`), every call head that program_writes reads as a write (open with a mode holding w, a, x or +; Path(...).write_text/write_bytes/unlink/touch/mkdir/rmdir/rename/replace and Path(...).open with such a mode; fs.writeFile/writeFileSync/appendFile/appendFileSync/createWriteStream/unlink/unlinkSync/rmSync/rmdirSync/mkdirSync/makedirs/rmtree/truncate; the os, fs, File, FileUtils, shutil and Dir methods it lists; unlink, mkdir, rmdir, file_put_contents; rename and the copy forms' destination) whose target argument is not a string literal (it starts with a name, a $, a parenthesis, an f-string prefix f"/f', a backtick template holding ${, a dot or any token other than a plain quote) is a denial under a run lease; for open, a non-literal mode argument is judged the same way, since the guard cannot read whether it writes.

The reason names the call as written in the program and ends with its own Next line, both pinned word for word in the test: `<call as written> writes a file the guard cannot name: the program gives its target through a variable, an expression or another call, so the guard cannot read where it writes` and `Next: name the file as a literal path in the program, or write it with the Edit tool (Write for a new file)`; the denial's first line is what the user sees (docs/guards.md), so it starts with the call text.

Where it applies: under a build or fix lease, for an agent of the owning session, on both inline forms (python3 -c, python -c, node -e, perl -e, ruby -e, php -r, lua -e, deno eval, bun -e; and heredocs such as python3 - <<'EOF' and node <<EOF); the same rule holds under the read-only qa and map leases (every write is refused there already) and the plan lease, as in_run judges every lease through one branch; outside a run programs stay unjudged (the R76 case stays). The R76 order is kept: a literal path outside the plan gets today's R76 refusal naming the path, a literal path inside the plan passes, and an unreadable target is refused even when lease.files is null (any project file allowed), because the guard cannot know where it lands.

What passes, each a case: a program that writes nothing (print, json.load(open(p)), open(p), open(p, 'r'), open(p, 'rb'), fs.readFileSync(p), Path(p).read_text()); python3 -m pytest and node --test; a heredoc fed to cat, tee or any non-interpreter holding the same program text is data (the 'a large heredoc is data' case in tests/hooks-guard.bats stays green); a program file run by name (python3 tools/x.py) is not read, as today; a Python string method named like a path method on a bare variable receiver (s.replace('a', 'b'), s.rename(...)) is not judged, because only the call heads program_writes reads are judged.

Tests, each shown red before the guard change, in tests/guard-interpreters.bats (R76's file, the area's one file; no new test file): the F323 shape first (a build lease whose files do not include tests/x.bats; a python heredoc that computes the path in a variable and opens it with 'w'); python open(path, 'w') from -c; open(f"{d}/x", 'w'); Path(d, 'x').write_text and (root / 'x').write_text; shutil.copy('a', dst); os.makedirs(d); node fs.writeFileSync(path.join(d, 'x'), ...) and a template literal with ${}; ruby File.write(p, ...); perl open(F, '>', $p); php file_put_contents($p, ...); and the passing cases above, plus a case asserting the whole reason and Next line. tests/refusal-next-step.bats's 'every block of the file guard and the Bash guard ends with its next step' case gets this block's line, as its header requires of every new refusal path.

Hot path: the new reading is one match over the program text (one regex, or folded into program_writes's regex); tools/bench-hooks.sh's interp.json program gains a line that writes through a variable, so the measured 'guard (interp)' and 'guard (interp, large record)' cases hold both shapes and stay within the 20 ms budget in the release run; tests/guard-cost.bats stays green (its label greps unchanged); no new subprocess, no file read by the guard.

Words: docs/guards.md's 'Programs that write files' paragraph replaces 'A path held in a variable cannot be read, so this stays a guard rail (see the first paragraph)' with the rule (a write whose target the guard cannot read is refused with the fix named; a program that writes nothing passes; a script file run by name is not read); docs/workflows.md's 'Every refusal and its next step' table gains a Guards row for it with the Next text above; plugin/agents/dev.md's writing rule (the 'Write only inside the project' line) says files are written with the Edit and Write tools, and a program that writes names its file as a literal path, because the guard refuses a program whose write target it cannot read. Each of the three is pinned by one case in tests/guard-interpreters.bats (docs/guards.md's paragraph, the table row's Next text, the Dev brief's sentence).

Standards: the guard-bash.jq header comment states the rule beside the heredoc-as-data rule (ledger D281) it refines; no hook answer allows (tools/check-hook-answers.sh, tests/standards.bats); JSON only through jq; the guard reads no file and runs no program.

phases.title: vbw apply refuses a bats case filter that names no case in the test file
phases.goal: When the Lead's plan carries a check that runs a bats test file with a case filter (bats --filter PATTERN, which runs only the test cases whose names match the pattern) and no case name in that file matches, vbw apply refuses before writing anything, naming the check and the file, so a new check is red because its cases fail, never because none exist; the Lead's brief says the failing cases are written at planning, before vbw apply.
criteria: The rule, in plugin/lib/cmd-apply.sh, in every mode (full apply, --add, --patch), judged on the document's checks after the merge and before record_update, after the two-owner and mixed-owner judgments (R211, R212, R215) in the same problem chain: for every check in the document whose run argv's command (the basename of its first word, env and timeout wrappers skipped) is bats and carries a case filter (--filter PATTERN, --filter=PATTERN or -f PATTERN), the kernel reads the case names (the quoted name of each @test "..." or @test '...' line) of the test files the argv names (the words ending in .bats that are not an option's value, and the .bats files directly under a directory word) as they stand in the project folder at apply time (the bytes the approval will freeze), and judges PATTERN as bats does (an extended regular expression, unanchored; grep -E, the pattern given with -e so one starting with - is not read as an option, stderr dropped); when no name of any of those files matches, vbw apply refuses before anything changes (the record byte-unchanged in the test), prefixed with the mode's name (R156).

The words, pinned word for word in the test: `C9 runs tests/x.bats with a case filter (--filter 'R220') that matches no case name in the file: the Lead writes the failing cases at planning, so a new check is red because its cases fail, never because none exist` and its own apply_next arm `Next: write the cases the filter names into tests/x.bats (each @test name matching the pattern), see them fail with the runner, then send the document again; or correct the pattern`; several files are named comma-separated in the file's place; the kernel never runs the runner at apply, it reads the file.

Edges, each a case: a test file missing from the project folder counts as a file with no case names and is refused by the same message with '(missing)' after its name; a pattern grep -E cannot parse matches nothing and is refused naming it; with several files a match in any one passes; a pattern matching at least one case passes; a check without a filter, a run whose command is not bats (pytest -k, node --testNamePattern, go test -run), --filter-tags and --filter-status are not judged and pass as today; the -f and --filter= forms are judged like --filter; a check the document resends unchanged is judged like any other (a full apply resends every check of the milestone); the R211/R212/R215 refusals keep their precedence when both apply.

Tests, each shown red before the code change, in the existing files of the area (no new test file): tests/apply-refusal-modes.bats holds the refusal and acceptance cases on a fixture bats file with named cases (full, --add and --patch each refused with the mode name; the record byte-unchanged); tests/refusal-next-step.bats's apply_refusal helper gets a case per mode for this refusal (its Next line differing from the fallback arm's text, R216) and the direct apply_next case gains this message, so a dropped arm turns the file red.

phases.title: The release run fails only on a real regression: scope judged by git ancestry, hook budgets judged against the runner's own speed
phases.goal: A CI release run (the full test and benchmark run on GitHub's machines) fails only when VBW's code really changed for the worse: never because two commits landed in the same second, and never because the machine running it is uniformly slow.
criteria: R221: in the proof's scope check (the check that every plan commit touched only the files its plan allowed), the record version a commit is judged against is the last commit of .vbw/record.json that is an ancestor of the judged commit in git history (a commit it descends from), never the one with the nearest clock time. The versions 'since' it are those after that ancestor in the record's own history.

R221: a regression test in tests/scope-of-its-time.bats makes a plan commit and then a record commit in the same second (GIT_COMMITTER_DATE set on both) where the later record version no longer allows the plan's file: vbw prove reports no scope violation. A second case gives a record commit made after the plan commit an earlier clock time (GIT_COMMITTER_DATE in the past): still no false violation, because ancestry, not time, picks the base. Both cases fail on the current code.

R221: a file that no record version since the ancestor version allows is still reported as a violation, and a decision that names the commit and the file still accepts one: the four existing cases of tests/scope-of-its-time.bats keep passing unchanged.

R221: the scope check's cost stays bounded: at most one extra git process per distinct candidate commit (a commit flagged for touching a file outside its plan), never a walk of the whole history per candidate; the R204 trace-count cases in tests/scope-history.bats (50 versus 500 commits) stay flat.
R221: docs/proof.md's Scope section (around line 635) says the base version is the last record commit the judged commit descends from, and no longer describes picking it by time.

R222: tools/bench-hooks.sh measures one fixed reference workload (the same work on every machine: a jq program of fixed size over fixed input, run as the hooks are run) on the same machine in the same run, before judging any case, and prints one line naming the reference's measured cost in ms, the nominal cost it is pinned against (measured on the nominal machines: an M1 Max Mac and GitHub's macOS runner, named in the script) and the ratio between them. The line's exact form is pinned by a test in tests/bench-limits.bats.

R222: a case at or under its absolute budget (20 ms per guard call, 60 ms status line, 10 ms hand-back) passes with today's line format; on a machine whose ratio is 1 or less the absolute budgets apply unchanged (a fast machine gets no looser and no tighter budget).

R222: on a machine whose ratio is above 1, a case above its absolute budget but at or under budget times ratio prints a line on stdout marked slow, naming the cost, the absolute budget, the ratio and the scaled budget; the bench exits 0 (slow, not failed). A case above budget times ratio prints ': OVER' on stderr and the bench exits 1: a real regression of one case still fails on a slow machine. Both are tested by driving the bench with a stand-in reference measurement (an environment override the tests use, as VBW_HOOK_BUDGET_MS is used today), and the one-more-measure rule (D517) judges against the scaled budget.

R222: the busy rule stays as documented: when sh and jq startup alone exceed the 20 ms hook limit, the bench reports busy, judges nothing and exits 0 (tests/bench-limits.bats cases at lines 180 and 209 keep passing).

R222: docs/guards.md (Budget, lines 267-280), docs/statusline.md (lines 73, 130, 162-170) and the hot-path rule in CLAUDE.md state the reference, the ratio and the slow report, with the absolute budgets kept as the meaning on a nominal machine; tests/bench-limits-docs.bats is edited to pin the new wording (cases edited, not stacked).

R222: the CI release run's benchmark output (shard 1 of each matrix entry in .github/workflows/ci.yml) shows the reference line, so a slow-runner report is visible in the log and is never a failed shard.

phases.title: jq 1.7 is the floor: every vbw command refuses an older jq and tells the user how to update
phases.goal: A user whose jq (the JSON tool VBW depends on) is older than 1.7 is told so by every vbw command and by vbw doctor, with the way to get a current one, and VBW's own jq programs are shown to run the same on jq 1.7 and 1.8.
criteria: vbw doctor with a jq older than 1.7 on PATH prints a fail line naming the installed version and 1.7 as the floor, and a fix line naming the jq releases page (github.com/jqlang/jq/releases) and, for Debian 12, the bookworm-backports package (apt install -t bookworm-backports jq); tested in a new tests/jq-floor.bats with a stand-in jq script on PATH that answers 'jq-1.6'. jq 1.7.0, 1.7.1 and 1.8.x each pass as 'jq <version>'. A missing jq keeps today's 'jq is missing' line.

D523: every vbw command (vbw status, vbw next, vbw init, vbw prove, any subcommand) run with a jq older than 1.7 stops before doing anything, prints doctor's one-line message with its fix to stderr, exits non-zero, and writes nothing (vbw init creates no .vbw folder). The check is one jq --version per kernel command, placed in plugin/bin/vbw after the libraries load and before the command dispatch; vbw doctor itself still runs so its fuller report shows.
D523: the hooks (plugin/hooks/*) and the status line (plugin/scripts/vbw-statusline.sh) gain no version check: a test asserts none of them calls jq --version, and the bench budgets are unchanged.

phases.title: A check that only runs a script by path is not rerun when an unrelated file lands at the project root
phases.goal: A check whose test does nothing but execute a script by its path (./greet.sh) is reused when a commit adds an unrelated file at the project root, because the project root's folder listing is no longer on its read list, while a test that itself lists a folder keeps that listing.
criteria: The cause is established by measurement before the fix is designed: the plan's evidence names which process reads the project root folder when a test runs ./greet.sh from the proof's clean copy (checks_exec runs the check's command through perl's exec, plugin/lib/checks.sh:141, so ./greet.sh goes through the kernel's shebang handling into /bin/sh, while sh greet.sh starts /bin/sh directly), shown with a system-call trace (fs_usage or dtruss on macOS, strace on Linux) or a controlled A/B run in the clean copy, on both macOS and Linux.

A regression test in tests/reads-listing.bats runs a check whose test is only ./greet.sh (an executable script with a shebang, run by path from the project root): the recorded read list (the files and folders a check read, kept per run) has no folder entry for the project root. The same holds for sh greet.sh (today's behaviour, kept). The ./greet.sh case fails on the current code.
After such a run, a commit that adds an unrelated file at the project root (for example NOTES.md) makes vbw prove reuse that check rather than run it again; the proof output names it as reused.

A test that lists a folder itself (ls, a glob such as *.txt, find .) keeps that folder's listing on its read list, and a file added to that folder still reruns the check: the R166 and R168 cases in tests/reads-listing.bats (lines 67-145) keep passing.

What VBW does about the start-up listing is one general mechanism, never a rule keyed on commands that start with ./ : preferred, it removes the cause (if the executed shell's start-up reads the folder to resolve its working directory, the check's environment gives it what it needs so no listing happens); only if the read cannot be prevented does VBW tell a start-up listing apart from a test's own, and the chosen way is written down with its limits.
docs/proof.md names the cause of the listing, what VBW does about it and that a listing the test itself asks for stays a read; tests/reads-docs.bats pins that wording.
The regression test passes on the macOS (/bin/bash 3.2) and Linux CI shards; T194 in the backlog is marked done when the phase is accepted.

phases.title: One `vbw mutate PLAN --run` at a time per plan
phases.goal: Two runs of the same plan's queued breaks can never run at once: the second refuses and names the first, a run that died never blocks the next, and the Dev knows to wait for a long run instead of starting it again.
criteria: plugin/lib/mutate-queue.sh: mutate_queue_run takes a per-plan marker under `.vbw/runtime/mutate-queue/<PLAN>/` (a `run.pid` lock in the pattern of record.sh vbw_lock_dir/vbw_lock_holder/vbw_lock_takeover) holding its own pid, before it reads any queue entry; the marker is removed when the run ends, on success, on a survivor, and on a `vbw_die` refusal (an EXIT trap), and is never a reason to skip removing queue entries.

A second `vbw mutate PLAN --run` while the marker's pid is alive (vbw_lock_alive) exits non-zero before reading, copying or deleting any queue entry and before recording anything, with a message beginning `vbw:` that names the running one (its pid and the command) and ends with a `Next:` line telling the Dev to wait for it to finish (a long run started in the background, its result read when it ends) and not start another; a bats case in tests/mutate-queue.bats writes a marker with a live pid (a sleeping child of the test) and asserts the exit status, the two message lines, the untouched queue folder and an unchanged record.

A marker whose pid is dead, empty or not a number does not block: the next run takes it over (as proofsteps.sh:45 does for the proof lock) and proceeds; a bats case writes a marker with a dead pid and asserts the run runs the breaks and leaves a marker with its own pid during the run and none after.

plans.title: Kernel: the loop step takes an item from milestone to ship, and knows where to stop
tasks: Opening an item (loop-step.sh): with no item in progress and a waiting item next, the step opens its milestone: `vbw milestone start TITLE` when the current one is shipped (or parked, P129), or `vbw milestone rename TITLE` when it is active with no requirements, TITLE being the item's requirement text (loop_item_text); then `vbw spec add auto|human TEXT` (loop_item_proof), `vbw todo` status in_progress, and the item becomes in_progress with milestone, head (git rev-parse HEAD after the commits) and its own cost baseline (every session's current figures). The functions of cmd-milestone.sh, cmd-spec.sh and cmd-todo.sh are called in-process, never a second vbw

Stops, judged in this order before anything else: a run lease of the caller's session → vbw next's run answer (a running workflow is never killed; the stop waits for its result); a lease of another session → stopped (`a run of another session (S) is open`); stopping → stopped (`stopped by the user (session S)`); with a ceiling in the default mode, the spend (loop_spend) at or above it → stopped (`ceiling reached: $X spent of a $Y ceiling`), or no figure → stopped (`cannot tell what was spent (no figure seen): vbw statusline on`); with --finish-item the comparison is made only before opening an item; with --no-ceiling never. A stop writes ended {at, reason} and commits

Actions: approve → loop_delegate (P127); accept → `vbw req skip` for each of detail.requirements (never accept, never reject); ship → `vbw ship` (also with detail.later: D256), the backlog entry done, the item shipped with its cost (loop_spend from the item's own baseline, null when no figure) and at, then the next item (opened the same call) or, with none waiting, ended {reason: `end of the list: N shipped, M parked`} and {action: done}; plan, build, fix, qa, prove and run → vbw next's answer plus the `loop` object (item {id, text, n, of}, spend, ceiling, word); escalate, unblock, scope, contract, convert, spec with an item in progress, or any other action → stopped with `ACTION needs you: INSTRUCTION (item T1, step ACTION)` (P129 replaces escalate, unblock and scope with retry and park)

The step loops over kernel-only actions inside one call until it reaches an agent step, a proof, done or stopped, reading the record afresh each time; every record change it makes is committed with the record (`chore(vbw): loop ITEM ACTION`); vbw next itself is never changed (tests/loop-cycle.bats compares the step's answer with vbw next --json and proves vbw next writes nothing)

plans.title: The shared slot store: every unit takes turns across the computer
tasks: New plugin/lib/slots.sh: the store is <vbw_claude_dir>/vbw/slots.json, one JSON document of held slots and waiting units, each naming its run (the vbw process, $$) and a wait order number; every change is one step under a short lock directory slots.lock/ holding its owner's pid in slots.lock/pid, taken over when that process is gone and, when the pid file is empty, only after a wait (as the gate's mutex); written atomically (temporary file in the same folder, then mv); the file is removed when nothing holds or waits, so an idle computer keeps no store

Turns (D339): a unit registers as waiting; on each look it drops the entries of runs whose process is gone, and takes a slot only when fewer than vbw_machine_limit are held and it is the chosen waiter: the waiting run holding the fewest slots, between equals the one that has waited longest; bash 3.2 only (no wait -n, no associative arrays)

Wire it into checks_unit_run: the slot is taken after checks_gate_enter and before checks_exec (the timeout starts with the command, never with the wait) and given back right after checks_exec, on pass, fail or timeout; the runner starts at most the smaller of check_jobs and the machine limit, so a unit only ever waits for other runs; the run's exit guard (Ctrl-C, TERM, vbw_die) removes this run's entries at once, and a runner lost without a result frees its entry like its gate places

Nested runs: each unit's command gets an environment marker naming the store it holds a slot in; a vbw run that finds the marker naming its own store takes no slot (the parent's unit covers it, D340) and so never waits for its parent; a run on another store (a test's own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR) takes slots as usual

Store unavailable: open the store once per command (checks_begin); when it cannot be created, read or written, or is damaged (not JSON, or not the store's shape), run with check_jobs as the only cap, never rewrite a damaged file, and print once on stderr 'vbw: the computer-wide limit was not in force: cannot write PATH; this run was limited by check_jobs (N) alone' or 'vbw: the computer-wide limit was not in force: PATH is damaged (delete it to restore the limit); this run was limited by check_jobs (N) alone'; then run the existing parallel suites (check-jobs-*, check-alone-*, check-wait-patient, gate-race, prove-parallel, prove-signal, runner-reads) under /bin/bash and bash 5

Keep the R148 wording (Do not run the project's test command or its quick command; only your fixes' checks; runs once, in the proof after this round; only the failing tests). No Dev prompt may contain 'vbw fix done F...'.

fixing.js, after every Dev has returned: the fixes of groups whose Dev reported done, in group order, go into one command, vbw fix done <ids> (with the VBW_SESSION_ID=<session> prefix when there is a session). With a session it is the first step of the closing Lead's prompt (label 'close run', effort lead.close), before vbw run confirm (still every fix of every group) and vbw run end; without a session a Lead agent of its own, labelled 'fix done', runs it before the workflow returns; with no done fix nothing runs it. The prompt says it may run past one shell command's 10-minute limit: if Claude Code moves it to the background, wait for it to finish and read its whole output (it ends with the two count lines) before anything else. The agent's schema adds fixdone ('ran' or 'failed'), closed (fix ids) and open ([{fix, reason}]); the workflow treats only an explicit 'failed' or no answer as a failure, so tests/workflow-closing.bats and tests/effort-workflows.bats keep passing.

fixing.js, the result: fixdone: {command, closed, open, left_out}, where left_out lists each fix of a blocked or interrupted group as {fix, status}; log each left-out fix with its status and each open fix with its reason. When the agent stops or answers fixdone 'failed', log 'run by hand:' with the exact vbw fix done command and set complete to false; otherwise complete is computed as before. Stay within the 1,500-line workflow budget.

plugin/agents/dev.md: in a fix, commit the fix and check it with vbw check on your fixes' checks, then return; never run vbw fix done: the workflow runs `vbw fix done F2 F3` once for the round, after every Dev returns (keep that multi-id example: tests/fix-many-docs.bats reads it); the recording line asks a plan for vbw plan done and a fix for its commit. plugin/agents/lead.md, Close a run: in a fix round, first the given vbw fix done, waited for to its end past a shell time limit, its whole output read, then confirm and end. Each agent stays at 900 words or fewer (lead.md is at 899 today: trim elsewhere without losing meaning).

plans.title: Name each proof copy after its owner, clear away copies whose owner has ended, and explain it in the proof guide
tasks: Record the owner when the copy is made: in proofcopy_make, create the folder in one step as .vbw/runtime/proof.$$.XXXXXX (mktemp -d), where $$ is the process id (pid) of the running vbw, so a copy never exists without its owner's pid in its name. The proof's own copy handling (proofcopy_remove, the interrupt guard, the proof.* patterns of proofcopy_warn_stale) keeps working unchanged.

Add proofcopy_sweep and call it at the start of proofcopy_create_slots, so vbw prove and vbw fix done both clean up before they make their own copies. For each .vbw/runtime/proof.* folder: a name proof.PID.REST (PID all digits, then a further part) belongs to PID; it is skipped while kill -0 PID succeeds (alive) and removed when it fails. A name with no owner part (proof.XXXXXX from an older VBW, even when XXXXXX is all digits) is removed only when it is more than 24 hours old (find FOLDER -maxdepth 0 -mmin +1440, which works on macOS and Linux), and kept otherwise.

Remove a dead copy safely: first claim it with one atomic mv to a new folder named after this process (.vbw/runtime/proof.$$.<unique part>), so a second cleanup running at the same moment sees a live owner and leaves it, and a cleanup killed partway leaves a folder whose owner has ended, which the next proof finishes. A failed mv (someone else took or removed it) is skipped without a word. Then chmod -R u+rwx (never follows links), rm -rf (never follows a link out of the copy) and git worktree prune, so git worktree list and .git/worktrees no longer name it; nothing from rm or git reaches the screen. If the folder is still there afterwards (a locked file), print exactly one stderr line, 'vbw: cannot remove the leftover proof copy <path from the project root>; remove it by hand', and go on with the proof. Keep the claim name, the 24-hour rule and the warning in proofcopy.sh's header comment.

docs/proof.md: in the 'vbw prove' steps, say the clean copy's folder is named after the process that made it (its owner, by process id), e.g. .vbw/runtime/proof.48213.k3Xa9Q; add a short section 'Leftover proof copies' next to 'Links left pointing into a proof copy': a proof killed outright can leave its copy; the next vbw prove or vbw fix done removes every leftover copy whose owner has ended, with its git worktree entry, never one whose owner still runs; a copy without an owner (older VBW) goes once more than 24 hours old; a copy that cannot be removed leaves the result unchanged and prints the one warning line.

Run bats tests/proof-copy-cleanup.bats and the other proof copy tests (proof-selfcontained, prove-signal, proof-stale-links, proof-copy-docs, fix-many) under /bin/bash; check shellcheck and the kernel's 7,600-line budget (tests/standards.bats).

tasks: Record shape, contract untouched: plugin/lib/record.jq accepts an optional plan field mutations, an array of entries: a break {rule: {req, text}} or {task: K} with what (one line), files, checks ({ID: "red" | "green"}), result ("red" | "survivor"), at, head (the commit it ran on) and, on a red break after a survivor of the same target, strengthened (paths); or a task with nothing to break {task: K, none: REASON, at}. plugin/lib/contract.sh leaves mutations out of the contract core, the shape and contract_doc, so recording a break never changes the fingerprint or the approval.

The command and its refusals: plugin/lib/cmd-mutate.sh with cmd_mutate, wired in plugin/bin/vbw (dispatch list, vbw help line, vbw_cmd_usage entry). Forms: vbw mutate PLAN Rn.k WHAT FILE... (rule k of requirement Rn, 1-based in that requirement's rules order, the numbering vbw show plan will show), vbw mutate PLAN taskK [--check ID]... WHAT FILE..., vbw mutate PLAN taskK --none REASON. Before anything runs, refuse with a message naming the next step and write nothing when: the plan, rule or task is unknown or the rule's requirement is not one the plan serves; a --check is not a check of the plan's requirements; --none is given with a rule or an empty reason; a FILE is not covered by the plan's files or is a check file; no FILE differs from HEAD (untracked counts); a check file of the checks to run differs from HEAD.

The run, isolated: copy the named files' broken bytes (or note a deletion) into the run's folder under .vbw/runtime, restore the named files to HEAD at once (before any check starts, also on error or interrupt through the guard), then in a proof copy of HEAD (proofcopy, removed at the end) run the target's checks unbroken (a rule: its own check; a task: the plan's requirements' checks, or only the --check ones) through checks_begin (not strict: check files waiting for approval still run) and checks_run_all, so machine slots and check_jobs hold. Any check that does not pass unbroken refuses, naming it, nothing written; an earlier break of this plan at the same HEAD that ran the same checks proves the unbroken pass and it is not run again. Then put the break into the copy and run the checks again.

Record and report: one locked record_update appends the entry; each check is red when it did not pass, green when it did; the result is survivor when every check stayed green: print a line naming survivor, the target (R2.1), the rule's text and the checks still passing, and exit 1; otherwise print each check red or green and exit 0. A red break after a survivor of the same target lists strengthened: the files of its checks whose content at this HEAD differs from the survivor's head. The named files are byte-identical to HEAD afterwards in every outcome.

Prove it: bats tests/mutate-command.bats and tests/mutate-isolation.bats pass under /bin/bash and bash 5; tests/standards.bats, tests/help-every-command.bats, tests/kernel-core.bats, tests/record-args-rule.bats and the approve and contract tests still pass. plans.title: Step history, expected length and the running step's note
tasks: History (new plugin/lib/steps.sh, replacing vbw_step_add in core.sh): each finished step goes into steps.json in the clone's git folder with its kind, start, end, seconds and, for a build or fix, its parts (plans or fixes in the run); the latest 50 of each kind stay, in time order; a missing, damaged or unwritable file never fails a step. JSON only through jq.

Expected length: kinds with parts take the median time per part over their latest 10 finished steps that recorded parts, times this step's parts; kinds without parts (plan, qa, map) the median of their latest 10; an even count takes the mean of the two middle values; fewer than 3 such steps gives no end time.

The note: The note (.vbw/runtime/step.json, written only by the kernel, atomically): {kind, run (the lease's run id, null for a proof of its own), session, pid (a proof of its own: its process, else null), started_at, ids (the run's plans, fixes or the phases QA checks), doing (plain words of what it does now: 'building P1.1, P1.2', 'checking P1', 'fixing F1', 'planning', 'mapping the project', 'proving 12 of 40 checks'; never the word QA), parts {done, total} or null, proof {done, total} or null, first_end, end (UTC ISO to the second, null for no basis), late}. vbw run start writes it (QA's ids are the phases vbw next would send to QA, by the same rule) after removing a note that is not live (its run is not the open run, or its proof process is gone); vbw run end records the step and removes the note.

vbw plan done adds one part done at once; when this run's own pace (time so far / parts done x parts left) ends after the first end time, end moves to that projection and late is true; it can move again and never goes earlier than first_end (D424).

vbw status --json gains step: the live note or null, plus minutes_late (whole minutes past first_end for a step without parts, else null); steps.sh also holds the one kernel wording of a step (jq defs) for vbw status, vbw next and vbw run start, used by P148.1.

plans.title: The step history records each unit of work: plans with tier, tasks and own seconds, the fix round's tier, planning's count, QA's phases
tasks: Build units in the note and the history: vbw run start build writes note.units = [{id, tier, tasks, seconds: null}] per plan (tier = the plan's phase tier at that moment, 'standard' when the phase has none; tasks = the plan's tasks count, 0 without tasks); step_plan_done stamps the plan's own seconds (run start to now) on its unit; step_record copies the units of plans done into the history entry (a plan left unfinished is no unit), beside parts as today

Other kinds in step_record: a fix run records fixes (its ids) and tier (the highest tier among the phases of the fixes' requirements; none when no phase serves them); a planning run records reqs (the active milestone's requirements not proven or accepted at run start); a QA run records phases [{id, tier}] from the note's ids and the record

step_expect KIND SIZE: SIZE is JSON (build: [{id, tier, tasks}] for the wave; fix: {tier}; plan: {reqs}; qa: [{id, tier}]; proof: {units: [names]}) and the function runs lib/steps-expect.jq (P149.2) as `jq -n --slurpfile h <history> --slurpfile runs <runs.json or an empty store> --arg kind K --argjson size SIZE -f`, printing seconds or nothing; step_start and step_next build SIZE from the record (phase tiers and tasks for the wave's plans; the fixes' highest tier; the open requirements count; QA phases with tiers; proof unit names check:ID, file:PATH, command:NAME from the proof plan's TODO_CHECKS, TF_TODO and TODO_COMMANDS), so next --json, the note and run start's sentence all use the new times with D425's wording unchanged

Entries written before (kind, seconds, parts) stay as they are and still feed the coarse rungs; the latest 50 of each kind are kept; a missing, damaged or unwritable steps.json or runs.json never fails a step and only means no end time yet; record-sized data reaches jq by pipe or --slurpfile only; bash 3.2 (tests/step-units-history.bats green, tests/step-expect.bats and tests/step-next.bats still green)

plans.title: The expectation ladders: one jq program turns the history, the runs store and a step's units into its expected seconds
tasks: A new lib/steps-expect.jq with the interface in its header: input none; $h[0] the history ({steps}) or null, $runs[0] the runs store ({runs}) or null, $kind, $size (as P149.1 defines); output one integer (seconds) or empty; medians of an even count take the mean of the two middle values; every list is 'the latest 10' by the history's order

Build: for each plan of $size the rungs in order: median seconds per task over the latest 10 plan units of its tier that recorded tasks > 0, times its tasks; else (fewer than 3) median seconds per plan over the latest 10 plan units of its tier; else median over the latest 10 plan units of any tier; the wave is the longest plan (never the sum); when fewer than 3 plan units exist in all, today's coarse rule on the builds that recorded parts (median seconds per part over the latest 10, times the wave's plan count, 3 builds at least); else nothing

Fix: median seconds of the latest 10 fix rounds whose tier equals $size.tier (3 at least), else of the latest 10 of any tier (entries without a tier included), else nothing; never multiplied by the fix count. Planning: median seconds per requirement over the latest 10 planning steps that recorded reqs > 0, times $size.reqs (3 at least), else the median seconds of the latest 10 planning steps (today's rule)

QA: each recorded QA step with phases gives one sample per phase (its seconds split over its phases, at the phase's tier); per phase of $size the median of the latest 10 samples of its tier (3 at least), else of any tier (3 at least); summed over the phases; with fewer than 3 samples in all, today's rule (median of the latest 10 QA steps, 3 at least); else nothing

Proof: over the latest 10 proofs that recorded units, ratio = seconds / sum(units[].seconds) (entries with a zero sum skipped); with 3 ratios at least, sum over $size.units of runs[name].seconds (a name the store does not know counts as the median of this proof's known units; no known unit at all gives nothing) times the median ratio, rounded; without 3 such proofs, today's rule on proofs with parts (median seconds per part over the latest 10, times the unit count, 3 at least); else nothing. Verified by hand against fixture files with jq -n --slurpfile; tests/step-ladder.bats and tests/step-proof-units.bats pass once P149.1 and P149.3 call it

rule.text: a plan's expected seconds are the median seconds per task over the latest 10 finished plans of its tier, times its tasks; another tier and older plans do not count
a build wave's expected time is its longest plan's, never the sum of its plans
with fewer than 3 finished plans of the tier that recorded tasks, a plan takes the median seconds per plan at that tier
with fewer than 3 finished plans of the tier, a plan takes the median seconds per plan of any tier
builds that recorded only parts still count by today's rule, the median seconds per plan times the wave's plans
with fewer than 3 plans in all there is no end time and no guess
with fewer than 3 finished plans of the tier that recorded tasks, a plan takes the median seconds per plan at that tier
a fix round with fewer than 3 rounds at its tier takes the median of any tier, and fewer than 3 rounds in all give no time
with fewer than 3 planning steps that recorded a count, planning takes the median planning time as today
QA's expected time is the sum over its phases of the median seconds per phase at the phase's tier, else per phase of any tier, else today's median QA time, else none
QA's expected time is the sum over its phases of the median seconds per phase at the phase's tier, else per phase of any tier, else today's median QA time, else none
a fix round's expected time is the median wall time of the latest 10 fix rounds at its tier, whatever the fix count

plans.title: The road: one jq program adds up everything still ahead in the milestone
tasks: The waves definition of vbw show contract (cmd-show.sh's waves($m)) moves into VBW_JQ_DEFS (record.sh) as the one wave schedule, used by show contract and by road.jq, so the road counts the waves exactly as the approval lists them

lib/road.sh: road_compute RECORD_JSON NEXT_JSON NOTE_JSON (NOTE_JSON empty when no step is live) prints the road or null; it is sourced by steps.sh (P150.2) and sources nothing itself; it uses step_expect (lib/steps-expect.jq) for every piece, VBW_STEP_DEFS for the clock words, and passes the record, the history and the runs store to road.jq by --slurpfile only

road.jq pieces, for the milestone's phases not passed by QA: each build wave still to build (plans not done or blocked, in wave order) at its longest plan's expected time; per phase one proof per remaining wave holding a plan of the phase (one proof at least when any of its checks is not passing in the evidence), sized by the phase's checks not yet passing and, with an approved single-file form, their test files; QA when needs_qa (the same rule as next.jq) at the QA rule for [{id, tier}]; the phase's usual fix rounds times (one fix round at the phase's tier + one proof of the phase's checks + one QA recheck); a live step (the note) contributes its current end instead of its own piece's first estimate

Usual fix rounds per tier: median of outcome.fix_rounds over the latest 10 finished phases (those with an outcome, in record order) of that tier, rounded; fewer than 3 such phases counts 0 and is named; before planning (no phases) and at spec or convert the road is the planning step alone, sized by the open requirements; with no milestone, a shipped or parked milestone, or nothing left to build, prove or check, the road is null

The sentence: 'Milestone end: about 2 h 10 min, until around 16:40, counting 2 fix rounds per deep phase (the usual here)'; tiers in the order deep, standard, express joined with ' and '; a tier with fewer than 3 finished phases reads 'counting no fix rounds: fewer than 3 finished deep phases here' (several lacking tiers: 'deep and standard phases'); durations under an hour 'about 12 min', from an hour 'about 2 h 10 min' ('about 2 h' when the minutes are 0); clock by step_clock ('tomorrow 00:20'); before planning 'Milestone end: planning about 2 min, until around 12:50; the rest follows once the work is planned'; any piece without a basis gives seconds and end null, basis 'VBW has timed fewer than 3 proofs here' (kinds: plans, fix rounds, proofs, planning steps, QA checks; the first missing in road order) and say 'no milestone end time yet (' + basis + ')'; basis otherwise names the pieces and the rounds' source; computed in one jq run; bash 3.2

It renders the pane (placement dock, scroll.bodyRows 30) at 100, 64, 60, 50 and 40 body columns on each of the eight tabs (h.press('tab-<id>')), then checks on the lines of screen(pane, columns): every tab shows exactly one of its two names whole on one line as '[ Now ]', '[ Timeline ]' or '[ Time ]' and so on (no line holds a cut name such as '[ Timelin' or a lone ']'); no line is wider than the columns; the head's rows (the lines above the body: scroll.bodyRows minus the body Box's height prop) equal the lines screen() draws for the head Box, gap included. Expected layouts (the fewest rows, then the full names over the short ones, then the portrait): 120, 100 and 91 columns: the eight full names on one row beside the portrait (85 cells of buttons and gaps, 6 of portrait); 90 and 85: the full names on one row, no Image; 69, 64, 60 and 54: the full names on two rows beside the portrait; 50 and 45: the full names on two rows, no Image; 44: the short names (Now Plan Proof Time Log Team Sess Cost) on two rows beside the portrait; 40: the short names on two rows, no Image (beside it they would take three). The portrait, when drawn, is an Image of 6 columns whose alt 'VBW' is whole. The fixed-height case (placement inline, no scroll) on a busy record is at most 30 lines and ends with '+N more · open Mission Control', the head counted the same way. It fails today (the stand-in draws no chrome and the pane puts every tab on one row).

tests/panel/r189/helpers/screen.mjs: a Button with no hotkey draws '[ ' + label + ' ]' (4 cells of chrome, as Claude Code 2.1.302 draws a tab button: the 2026-10-19 capture shows '[ Now ] [ Plan ]'); a Button with a hotkey keeps '[k] label', the same 4 cells of width. Update the file's header comment. Every check that lists screen.mjs is re-approved once before the proof (the pre-proof approval names them).

plugin/hooks/panel-pane.js: named constants BUTTON_CHROME = 4 (the '[ ' and ' ]' Claude Code draws around a button's label) and TAB_GAP = 1 (the cell between tab buttons); PORTRAIT_DRAWN_ROWS = 3 (the Image's rows). measure()'s Button case counts BUTTON_CHROME. tabRows(names, width): the tabs packed in order into whole rows, each row holding as many whole buttons as fit (first-fit in order gives the fewest rows), never splitting a name; a width narrower than one button still gives one button per row. layout(width, portraitWanted): every candidate (with the portrait, its 6 columns taken from the width, and without; the full names and SHORT) ranked by the fewest rows, then the full names over SHORT, then the portrait over none, so the portrait never costs a row or a full name; it is a candidate only under today's conditions (Image, a portrait path, rows < 1 or rows >= PORTRAIT_ROWS). The tabs are a column Box of row Boxes (flexDirection row, columnGap TAB_GAP, flexShrink 0), one Button per tab, no flexWrap and no flexShrink on the row, so Ink never squeezes the portrait or a label. headRows = max(portrait ? PORTRAIT_DRAWN_ROWS : 0, tab rows) + (gap ? 1 : 0), used by both the reported-height branch (body height rows - headRows) and the fixed-height branch (FIXED_ROWS - headRows - 1 for the fold line). Remove HEAD_ROWS and tabsWidth. Update the file's header comment (eight tabs, whole rows).

Fix the header comment about 53 columns. The file goes through the pre-proof approval if a check lists it.

Run node --test tests/panel/r199/tab-rows.test.mjs, tests/panel/wiring.test.mjs, tests/panel/pane.test.mjs and the r189, r190, r191, r192 folders; run bash tools/bench-panel.sh once and put the render and tick figures in the plan note (tests/panel-bench-render.bats's budget is judged at release).

plans.title: A clock inside the proof: five step timers and the two report lines
tasks: New plugin/lib/prooftime.sh: prooftime_clock (seconds with milliseconds: date +%s.%N where %N is honoured, else perl Time::HiRes), prooftime_begin (a per-process scratch file under .vbw/runtime, guarded), prooftime_add STEP SECONDS (appends, so a unit's subshell can add its own seconds) and prooftime_total (one JSON object {planning, copies, tracking, saving, record, wall} in seconds), plus prooftime_lines that renders the two report lines from an evidence-shaped object: units are the checks that did not wait, the commands that were not skipped and are not of_files, and the test files; N are those without reused; a unit's reason is its why, or each of the proof's causes when it has none; at most three, most frequent first, ties in the units' order; 'none' when N is 0; minutes with one decimal.

plugin/lib/checks.sh: in checks_unit_run, time reads_reset and reads_collect with prooftime_clock and add both to the proof's tracking step (nothing when no proof timer is open, so vbw check is unchanged).

plugin/lib/cmd-prove.sh: time planning (proofreuse_plan, proofcauses_find, testfiles_plan, prove_plan_all), copies (proofcopy_create_slots), saving (proofreuse_save, testfiles_save) and record (the evidence record_update); the evidence gains own (the split; own.record is added by the second record_update, after the wall time is read) and causes (the whole-proof causes, [] when none); the two lines print just before the verdict line (proved / not proved), from the record's evidence. tests/prove-own-work.bats prove cases red before, green after.

plugin/lib/cmd-fix.sh: the same timers; the fixes are judged and the record written before anything prints (the refusal lines are buffered and printed where they print today, so the output order is unchanged); the two lines print right after 'test files: N ran, M reused', from the round's results, reuse map and causes; zeros and 'none' when nothing was judged. tests/prove-own-work.bats fix done cases green; fix-done-output.bats, fix-many.bats, machine-wait-line.bats, prove-summary.bats green.

plans.title: The stand-in large project, the measurement script and the before decision
tasks: tools/measure-proof-speed.sh (maintainers only, like tools/measure-fix-round.sh): the generator. Options --files N --folders N --units N (defaults 5000, 500, 200) and --generate DIR (build the stand-in at DIR in the caller's environment, print 'fixture: stand-in (F files, D folders, U units)' and stop). A two-level folder tree, small text source files; units are half approved checks (sh tests/c_N.sh, files tests/c_N.sh) and half test files tests/t_N.sh under the form 'sh {file}' with files tests/t_*.sh; each unit reads a handful of source files; every fourth unit writes 300 files into the git-ignored .buildcache/ (named in .gitignore; not a build-folder name, so the clean copy carries it) and the unit after it reads them back; one plan of R1 done, contract and commands approved, everything committed. No word, path or code of any real user project.

The measurement: an isolated HOME and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR under VBW_MEASURE_DIR (default .vbw/runtime/scratch/measure-proof-speed, rebuilt each run); a jq wrapper first on PATH for the measured commands that runs the real jq and appends its children's CPU seconds (the shell's times builtin) and one count line; vbw prove timed by a HiRes clock; then one line appended to one source file some units read, an open fix F1 of R1 written into the record, vbw fix done F1 timed; then vbw next --json timed; a once-a-second sampler keeps the largest size of .vbw/runtime/proof.*/reads/written.json seen; the expected reuse count is read from runs.json before the fix round: the units whose read lists do not contain the changed file.

Output, one 'name: value' line each, exactly these names: fixture, files, folders, units, 'prove: ' followed by each of the two report lines, prove wall seconds, prove own seconds, prove planning seconds, prove copies seconds, prove tracking seconds, prove saving seconds, prove record seconds (from evidence.own), 'fix done: ' followed by each of its two lines, fix done wall seconds, fix done own minutes (from its line), reused, reused expected, jq cpu seconds, jq processes, store bytes, written lists bytes, next seconds. tests/measure-proof-speed.bats green.

Run the script at the default size on this Mac and record the before numbers with vbw decide: text starting 'Proof speed before (M42) on this Mac:' and carrying 'stand-in (F files, D folders, U units)', 'prove W s wall', 'own work O s (P%)', 'fix done after one file: reused N of M units', 'jq C CPU s in K processes', 'store B bytes', 'written lists B bytes', 'vbw next T s', then 'planning A s, copies B s, read tracking C s, saving D s, record E s', then '(a) confirmed|cleared', '(b) ...', '(c) ...', '(d) ...' with one clause each saying what the numbers showed; why: the script, its size and the date. tests/proof-speed-before.bats green.

plans.title: Read tracking in a fixed number of processes; a written-file store that grows with names
tasks: Red first: tests/reads-fixed-jq.bats and tests/reads-written-store.bats fail on the current code (one jq and one sha256 per listed folder; one copy of the list per written file).

reads_collect fingerprints: one jq builds every listed folder's listing text (the compact JSON [path, names], names from one pass over the tracked paths through a parent-to-names map, so the work grows with files plus folders), bash writes one scratch file per listed folder with no process (printf and a redirection), one sha256sum or shasum call fingerprints all of them, one jq assembles the list; bytes identical to today's list.

written.json becomes {lists: {<run id>: {files, dirs, git}}, files: {<path>: [<run id>, ...]}}: a run that wrote files stores its list once under a fresh id (a counter in the state folder); each written path gains that id; a later run that reads a written path inherits the union of the lists its ids name; reads_reset takes the wlist from .files and creates the empty store in the new shape.

plans.title: Reuse planning and saving in batches: fixed store and record reads, one diff-tree per tree
tasks: Red first: the two process-count tests of tests/proof-plan-batch.bats fail on the current code (today vbw next on 50 units: 100 git diff-tree and 575 jq processes).

Fingerprints in one pass: proofreuse_fingerprints RECORD writes each unit's canonical bytes (a check's approved definition; a command's time limit and argv; a test file's limit and argv) to one scratch file per unit, runs one sha256sum or shasum call, and keeps the map unit -> fp in a scratch JSON file that planning, saving and stamping read (proofreuse_check_fp, proofreuse_command_fp and testfiles_fp stay as one-unit fronts giving the same values).

Planning in one pass: one git diff-tree per distinct recorded tree (shared with proofcauses_files, which today runs one per store entry) and one git ls-tree -r of HEAD for every listed-folder fingerprint, then one jq that applies the one reuse rule to every unit (checks, commands, test files) and gives the reuse set, the todo list and the reasons in today's words and precedence; proofreuse_reason stays the one-unit front over the same jq rule (proofreuse-rule.bats); testfiles_plan and cmd_fix use the batch.

Saving and stamping in one jq each: proofreuse_save, testfiles_save, prove_stamp and testfiles_finish take the fingerprint map and the results by file; the store and the record are read a fixed number of times per proof.

proof-reuse.bats, proofreuse-rule.bats, fix-reuse.bats, proof-selective.bats, proof-causes.bats, proof-cause-tree.bats, proofcauses-lib.bats, fix-done-output.bats, prove-summary.bats, prove-testfiles.bats, prove-own-work.bats and proof-plan-batch.bats green.

plans.title: One git walk finds exact undos; the proof leaves them unjudged and lists them
tasks: Red first: tests/scope-undone.bats and the three R204 tests of tests/park-ids.bats fail on today's code (62 git processes for 5 commits against 107 for 50; no evidence.undone). plugin/lib/cmd-prove.sh, prove_scope: replace the walk plus one git diff-tree per trailer commit with one `git log --topo-order --no-renames --raw --no-abbrev -z --format='%H%x1f%(trailers:key=VBW-Plan,valueonly)'` (stderr dropped, as today). The -z stream is NUL-separated: a commit header `<hash>\x1f<trailer values, newline-separated>` then, for a commit that changes files, a leading newline and raw entries `:<old mode> <new mode> <old blob> <new blob> <status>` NUL `<path>` NUL (a merge commit lists nothing, as git diff-tree lists nothing for it today). Read it with `read -r -d ''` loops in bash 3.2 (no mapfile, no associative arrays), never grep or sed on JSON, never reading any file content. Per commit keep: the hash, the first VBW-Plan value (as today), and per path its old pair (mode, blob) and new pair (mode, blob). The park's reverts are read as today (`.loop.items[].reverts`, one `git log -1` per recorded revert: bounded by the record, not by the history). One commit: perf(P165.1): one git log walk builds the scope check's per-commit pairs.

The mirror-image match, in the same prove_scope, newest first in the walk's order. A commit B is the mirror image of an earlier commit A when both change exactly the same set of paths and, for every path, B's old pair equals A's new pair and B's new pair equals A's old pair (a file A added is deleted by B; a file A deleted is added back with the same mode and blob; a mode-only change is put back). Compute per commit a forward key (the sorted lines `path old-mode old-blob new-mode new-blob`, hashed with vbw_sha256 or compared as one string) and a backward key (the same lines with the pairs swapped): B mirrors A exactly when B's backward key equals A's forward key. Standing: a commit stands while no later standing commit has taken it; each standing commit takes at most one commit, the nearest earlier one it mirrors, as the walk reaches that earlier commit (the nearest unconsumed later standing commit whose backward key equals the earlier one's forward key takes it); before a pair counts, one `git merge-base --is-ancestor EARLIER LATER` confirms the earlier commit is an ancestor of the later one (a candidate that fails is skipped and the next nearest is tried). A taken commit no longer stands, so it takes nothing and clears nothing: a revert of a revert leaves the original standing and judged; a re-apply after a revert takes the revert (which carries no trailer) and is itself judged when it carries a trailer; apply, undo, apply, undo pairs newest first and leaves all four unjudged. Judged set: a commit whose trailer names a plan of the current milestone is judged (today's covers/survivor_files jq, today's wording and order) unless it was taken, unless it is a park-cleared original, or unless it is a standing commit that took a commit carrying a VBW-Plan trailer (the pair cancels). No message, trailer or author is read for the match itself. One commit: feat(P165.1): the scope check leaves a commit exactly undone by a later standing commit unjudged.

Parallel proof can break the check gate under load. plugin/lib/checks.sh line 102 creates the lock owner file with printf > $g/mutex/pid right after mkdir; a waiting check that reads that file while it is still empty treats the owner as dead and runs rm -rf on a live lock (the gate's takeover test passes an empty pid to checks_gate_live). Parallel proof makes this window common. The Linux suite already hit it (mutex/pid: No such file or directory). Evidence: tests/gate-race.bats (untracked, not committed) fails 2 of 3 on HEAD: 'a lock whose owner file reads empty is not taken over at once' (the check took the lock: C1 pass 0s) and 'the owner write never prints an error' (checks.sh:102 matches). Fix: do not take over on an empty owner file until a wait has passed, write the owner file so a vanished lock prints nothing, commit the test. Minor: plan P56.2 lists plugin/lib/cmd-prove.sh but no commit touched it.
